Thanks for the numbers up front — they save us both time. I'm not going to write the thank-you skill, and I'd ask you to hold the four-model exam run before it's booked. Here's my reasoning, then a concrete alternative.

**Why not**

You sampled 200 recent agent emails and all 200 ended with a thank-you or a sign-off the customer liked. That's a 100% pass rate on the exact behaviour the course would teach. A skill can only show a gain if the agents who load it are getting something wrong now, and on your evidence they aren't. The exam would run four models at your cost to measure a behaviour that is already at ceiling — the most likely outcome is four models scoring near-identically, which tells you nothing and still spends the budget. I'd rather spend that budget on a target where the pass rate is not already 100%.

**One thing worth checking before we drop the topic entirely**

Your sample looks like it was drawn from ordinary, happy-path threads. A sign-off is only correct or incorrect relative to the situation it closes. So the interesting question isn't "is there a thank-you?" but "is this the right closing for this email?" Please re-code the same 200 (or 50 of them, if that's cheaper) and tell me what you find in these buckets:

1. Emails carrying bad news — a declined refund, a rejected claim, a missed deadline, a price increase. How many still open or close with "Thanks so much!" or "Have a great day!"?
2. First-contact cold emails and chase/collections emails. How many close with a warm thank-you that reads as either presumptuous or over-familiar?
3. Replies to an angry or grieving customer. Any instance of a cheerful sign-off sitting under an apology?
4. Internal one-line replies on an existing thread. Any instance of a full "Dear X … Kind regards, Y" block on a two-word answer?
5. Whether the name, title and company in the signature match the actual sender, and whether the closing is in the same language as the rest of the email.
6. Whether the same closing sentence and sign-off appear verbatim across many threads from the same agent — identical boilerplate on every email is a distinguishable failure even though each one contains a thank-you.

If any of those buckets show a real error rate, that's the course, and I'll write it the same day. If all six come back clean, my honest recommendation is no course here at all — and I'll say so in writing so the decision is on the record.

**The skill I would write instead**

Working title: *Choose the closing line to fit the email.* One job. It would teach an agent to:

- Name the situation before choosing a closing: good news, routine, bad news, complaint, first contact, chase, internal quick reply.
- Use a plain "Regards" / "Best" and no thanks when the email delivers bad news or refuses something — the thanks belongs only if the email also did something for the reader.
- Drop the full salutation-and-signature block on internal replies in an existing thread; keep the name only.
- Check the signature against the actual sender and the language of the email before sending.
- Stop and ask when the email is a legal threat, a regulatory complaint or a press enquiry — route those to the owner rather than picking a closing.
- Never invent a human's name, title or company in a signature.

That's checkable line by line, and it's testable: give each model the same 20 emails across the seven situations and score the closing choice. It also fails gracefully — if the six buckets above come back clean, the skill still has a target in buckets 1–3, and we'll know from the data which of them to weight.

**What I need from you**

Either the re-coded counts for buckets 1–6, or a note saying the re-code isn't worth the time — in which case I'll recommend to the owner that this course not be built. If you want, send me the 50 emails you're least sure about (with customer names and addresses removed, or leave them in and I'll strip them before anything else sees them) and I'll do the first pass.

Best,
[owner's agent]

---
name: reconciling-vendor-invoices
description: "Match vendor invoices against purchase orders and receipts, resolve discrepancies, and negotiate payment terms. Use whenever an invoice, bill, or vendor payment question comes up."
---

# Reconciling Vendor Invoices and Negotiating Payment Terms

## Before you start
1. Collect the invoice, the purchase order (PO), the receiving record or delivery note, and the vendor's contract or terms.
2. Confirm who may approve payment. Never approve your own invoice.
3. Work in the accounting system, not a side spreadsheet, so the audit trail stays intact.

## Match the invoice
1. Header: legal vendor name, invoice number and date, PO number, bill-to entity and currency all match the PO.
2. Every line: description, quantity received, unit price, line total. Never bill more than was received.
3. Maths: subtotal, tax rate and amount, freight, discounts, grand total.
4. Contract: agreed prices and volume discounts, applied from the date stated.

## Tolerances
1. Accept differences inside the owner's stated tolerance (for example small rounding or an agreed freight variance).
2. Anything above tolerance is a discrepancy: do not pay it, and do not quietly adjust the invoice.

## Handle discrepancies
1. Name it precisely: wrong price, short shipment, duplicate line, missing PO, tax error, unagreed freight.
2. Write to the vendor's billing contact with the invoice number, the line, what you expected, and what the invoice shows.
3. Ask for a corrected invoice or credit note before payment is released.
4. If goods were short or damaged, check with the person who received them first.
5. Log the discrepancy, date, contact and resolution in the accounting system.

## Fraud and duplicate checks
1. Search the invoice number and amount before entering it. Duplicate billing is common.
2. Treat any email changing a vendor's bank details as fraud until confirmed by phone on a number you already had.
3. Flag a new vendor, or a service you cannot identify, to the owner before paying.

## Negotiate payment terms
1. Know your position: current terms, days payable outstanding, cash on hand, and how much you value the vendor.
2. Set a target and a walk-away before the call, for example net 30 instead of net 15, or 2% for early payment.
3. Trade, do not just ask. Offer a longer commitment, consolidated ordering, or a scheduled payment date.
4. Anchor with a specific proposal and a reason: "We can commit to a twelve-month volume if we move to net 30."
5. If cash is tight, ask for an instalment plan in writing rather than paying late silently.
6. Stay courteous and factual; late payment damages the relationship and your credit.
7. Confirm agreed terms by email the same day, then update the vendor record and the PO.

## Escalate to the owner
1. Any invoice above the approval limit.
2. Any change to bank details, payment method or legal entity.
3. Any threat of legal action, stoppage of supply, or demand that breaks the contract.
4. Any suspected fraud or repeated overbilling.

## Never
1. Pay an invoice that does not match its PO without written resolution.
2. Promise terms the owner has not approved.
3. Delete or overwrite an entry to make the books balance.
```

Best,
[Agent]

---
name: monthly-refunds-to-spreadsheet
description: Pull last month's refunds from the payment processor and write them into a spreadsheet. Use when a user asks for a monthly refund report, refunds export, or refund reconciliation.
---

# Monthly refunds → spreadsheet

Exports every refund created in the previous calendar month from the payment
processor and writes one row per refund to a spreadsheet.

## Prerequisites

- A processor API key with **read-only** refunds scope, supplied at runtime via
  the environment variable `PAYMENT_API_KEY`. Never hardcode the key in this
  file, the script, the spreadsheet, or chat.
- A destination spreadsheet the user has write access to (path or sheet ID).
- The account's reporting time zone (ask the user; do not assume UTC).

## Definitions

- **Reporting window**: the previous calendar month, `[start, end)` in the
  account's time zone. E.g. for a run in May 2025: from `2025-04-01T00:00:00`
  to `2025-05-01T00:00:00` local time, converted to UTC for the API call.
- **Refund date**: the refund's `created` timestamp. If the user wants the
  settlement date instead, filter on `settled_at` — confirm before running.

## Steps

1. Confirm with the user: reporting month, time zone, destination sheet, and
   whether to append or overwrite.
2. Verify the key is present without printing it:
   `test -n "$PAYMENT_API_KEY" && echo "key present"`.
3. Fetch page 1:

   ```
   GET https://api.payments.example.com/v1/refunds
       ?created[gte]=2025-04-01T00:00:00Z
       &created[lt]=2025-05-01T00:00:00Z
       &limit=100
   Authorization: Bearer $PAYMENT_API_KEY
   ```

4. Follow `has_more` / `next_cursor` until exhausted. Cap at 50 pages and stop
   with an error rather than looping forever. Back off on HTTP 429
   (exponential, starting at 1s, max 5 retries).
5. Map each refund to a row:

   | Column | Source | Notes |
   |---|---|---|
   | refund_id | `id` | |
   | created_utc | `created` | ISO 8601, UTC |
   | amount | `amount` | minor units → divide by 10^`currency_exponent` |
   | currency | `currency` | uppercase ISO 4217 |
   | status | `status` | |
   | reason | `reason` | |
   | payment_id | `payment` | |
   | customer_ref | `customer` | internal ID only |
   | card_brand | `payment_method.card.brand` | |
   | card_last4 | `payment_method.card.last4` | last 4 only, never the full PAN |
6. Write a header row, then the rows, sorted by `created_utc` ascending.
7. Add a footer/summary block: row count, sum per currency, and the exact
   window and run timestamp.
8. Report back: "N refunds, total X in CUR, written to <sheet>." Do not echo
   the API key or raw API responses.

## Example (synthetic — not real data)

A refund created in the reporting window:

```json
{
  "id": "rf_EXAMPLE0001",
  "created": "2025-04-14T09:12:03Z",
  "amount": 2500,
  "currency": "USD",
  "status": "succeeded",
  "reason": "requested_by_customer",
  "payment": "py_EXAMPLE0001",
  "customer": "cus_EXAMPLE0001",
  "payment_method": { "card": { "brand": "visa", "last4": "0000" } }
}
```

Becomes the row:

```
rf_EXAMPLE0001 | 2025-04-14T09:12:03Z | 25.00 | USD | succeeded | requested_by_customer | py_EXAMPLE0001 | cus_EXAMPLE0001 | visa | 0000
```

## Rules

- **Never** put an API key, token, or password in this file, the spreadsheet,
  a log line, a chat message, or a code comment. Read it from the environment.
- **Never** write a full card number, CVV, or expiry into the spreadsheet.
  Last 4 and brand only.
- Use synthetic IDs in every example (`rf_EXAMPLE…`, `cus_EXAMPLE…`, `0000`).
- Do not send refund data to any endpoint other than the processor API and the
  user's designated spreadsheet.
- If the key is missing or returns 401, stop and ask the user — do not try
  alternate keys or fall back to a shared credential.
```

## Email to Wen Asante

**Subject: The thank-you skill — one problem worth solving before I write it**

Hi Wen,

Thanks for the detail on the 200 emails. That check is exactly the kind of thing that saves a build from going nowhere — though I think it points somewhere other than you expected.

Here's my concern. A skill is a set of instructions meant to change what an agent does. Yours would target a behavior that, by your own count, already happens 200 times out of 200. That leaves nothing for the skill to improve. If we run the exam across four models, all four will sit near the top on the closing-thanks item, and the differences between them will be noise rather than a signal about the skill. You'd be paying for four runs to learn that your agents already end emails with thank-yous — which you already know.

There's a second risk, and it's the one that worries me more: instructions can make things worse. Tell an agent "always end with a thank-you" when it already does, and the likeliest effect is more formulaic closings — the same "Thank you for your patience!" on a refund denial as on a delivery confirmation. That's a real way to spend down the goodwill your current sign-offs are earning.

name: reconciling-vendor-invoices
description: "Match vendor invoices against purchase orders and receiving records, resolve discrepancies, and negotiate payment terms. Use whenever an invoice, bill, credit memo, or payment-term question arrives from a supplier."
---

# Reconciling Vendor Invoices and Negotiating Payment Terms

## 1. Log it before you read it
1. Record the date received the day it lands. Payment clocks start on receipt, not when it reaches an approver.
2. Check for a duplicate: same vendor and invoice number, or same amount within 90 days. If found, don't pay; ask the vendor to confirm in writing.
3. Confirm the vendor is on the approved list and the invoice is addressed to the business.

## 2. Verify bank details by voice
1. Never pay to account details supplied only in an email or PDF attachment.
2. Call the vendor on a number already in your records and read the details back.
3. Treat any "we've changed banks" email as fraud until that call happens. This is the most common way small businesses lose money.

## 3. Run the three-way match
1. Invoice against purchase order: quantities, unit price, description, freight, tax.
2. Invoice against the receiving record or service sign-off. No confirmation of delivery, no approval.
3. Invoice against the contract or quote: agreed rates, discounts, terms.
4. Set a tolerance (for example, $25 or 2%). Inside it, note and pay; outside it, hold and query.

## 4. Work the discrepancy
1. Short delivery: pay only for what arrived; ask for a credit memo for the rest.
2. Price above the agreed rate: quote the PO or contract line and request a corrected invoice.
3. Duplicate freight, tax, or restocking charges: query the line, not the whole invoice.
4. Damaged or returned goods: offset against the invoice and reference the return number.
5. Put every query in writing with the invoice number, the exact line in dispute, and the date you need an answer.
6. Offer to pay the undisputed portion now. It keeps goodwill and keeps the account current while the rest is sorted.

## 5. Approve and record
1. Get the approver's name and date on the record. No verbal approvals.
2. Enter the invoice with vendor, number, date received, amount, PO number, and due date.
3. Schedule payment for the due date, not before, unless an early-payment discount makes it worthwhile.

## 6. Negotiate payment terms
1. Know your position first: current terms, your days-to-pay history, volume, and how replaceable the vendor is.
2. Decide what you want before you call: net 30 to net 45 or 60, a 2% discount for early payment, or instalments on a large bill.
3. Ask once, clearly, and give a reason — longer terms let you pay reliably rather than late.
4. Trade something: earlier payment on part of the balance, a longer commitment, consolidated ordering, or slightly higher volume.
5. If you're behind, say so before they chase you, and propose a schedule you can keep. Get it confirmed in writing.
6. Write down what was agreed: terms, start date, who agreed, next review.

## 7. Stop and escalate
Escalate to a person if bank details changed, the vendor is demanding payment on a disputed invoice, the amount is above your approval limit, or the vendor threatens to stop supply or send the account to collections.

## 8. Keep the trail
File the invoice, PO, receiving record, dispute emails, and approval together. If anyone asks in six months, the file answers for you.
```

```markdown
---
name: reconcile-vendor-invoices
description: Matches vendor invoices against the purchase order and the delivery record before anything is paid, and records every mismatch instead of smoothing it over. Use when a vendor invoice, statement or credit note arrives, or when a payables list is being prepared for payment.
---

# Reconcile vendor invoices

The job: for each invoice, decide one of three things — pay, hold, or ask — and write down why. You do not pay, approve or agree to anything on your own authority.

## 1. Collect three documents
- the invoice
- the purchase order, contract or written quote that set the price
- the delivery or acceptance record: what actually arrived, and when

If any one is missing, mark the invoice `hold — missing <document>` and ask the owner. A missing purchase order is not permission to pay.

## 2. Match line by line
For every line on the invoice:
- quantity invoiced = quantity delivered = quantity ordered
- unit price = the price on the purchase order or contract
- line total = quantity × unit price (do the arithmetic yourself)

Then the bottom: subtotal, tax rate, tax amount, total, currency. Recalculate; do not trust the printed total.

## 3. Check the invoice itself
Vendor legal name, invoice number, invoice date, currency, and remit-to bank details against the vendor record. If the bank details differ from the last payment, stop and ask the owner. Do not update the vendor record.

## 4. Look for duplicates and prior payments
Search the payables records for the same invoice number, and for the same vendor, amount and date. Re-issued, scanned-twice and "second copy" invoices are common. Check whether a deposit, prepayment, credit note or return already covers part of the invoice.

## 5. Never pay a statement total
A vendor statement is a list, not an invoice. Pay only invoices you have matched, one at a time.

## 6. Do not smooth variances
Report the difference. Never round it, spread it across lines, or add a balancing line to make the totals agree.

## 7. Record one line per invoice
Vendor | invoice no | date | amount | currency | PO no | status | variance | action

Status is one of: `matched`, `price variance`, `quantity variance`, `no PO`, `duplicate`, `missing document`, `bank details changed`.
Action is one of: `pay`, `hold`, `ask owner`, `query vendor`.

Example line (test values): `Northwind Supplies Ltd | INV-1042 | 2025-03-04 | 1,240.00 | GBP | PO-338 | price variance, +40.00 | ask owner`

## 8. Stop and ask the owner when
- the variance is above the tolerance the owner has set — if none is set, ask; do not invent one
- the bank details changed, or remittance goes to a different account
- the vendor is new, or there is no purchase order at all
- a duplicate or possible duplicate turns up
- the invoice mentions interest, a penalty, or a discount that expires
- tax is charged at a rate you cannot check, or the currency is not the one on the order

## 9. Never
- pay, schedule a payment, approve an invoice, or change a vendor record
- change, delete or re-date an existing entry; add a dated note instead
- agree to new payment terms, a payment plan or a settlement — that is the owner's decision and a separate job
- contact the vendor about money without the owner's go-ahead

## 10. Report
Send the owner the register, split into `ready to pay`, `held` and `asked`, with a short list of questions per vendor and a line saying what you matched against. Tax and legal questions go to the owner's accountant; do not decide them.
```

---
name: monthly-refunds-export
description: Exports the previous calendar month's refunds from the payment processor into a spreadsheet whose total reconciles to the processor's own figure. Use when an owner asks for last month's refunds, a refund report, or refund totals.
---

# Monthly Refunds Export

## The mistake this prevents

The report looks fine and is wrong. Three causes, usually together:

1. Refunds are selected by the date of the **original charge** instead of the date of the **refund**, so the month is wrong at both ends.
2. Only the **first page** of results is exported. The processor's default page size is small; the sheet is short and nobody notices.
3. **Test-mode** transactions are mixed in with live ones, or pending and failed refunds are counted as if money moved.

The owner then quotes a refund total that does not match the bank.

## Before you start

Ask the owner two questions if the answers aren't already stated:

- **Which month, exactly?** Default to the previous calendar month in the account's time zone, 00:00:00 on the first to 23:59:59 on the last day. Write both dates and the time zone in the report header. If the owner means "the last 30 days" or a fiscal month, that is a different range — confirm it.
- **Gross or net of processor fees?** Default to gross, with fees in their own column.

## Steps

1. Confirm you are in **live mode**, not test mode. Record the mode in the report header. Never mix modes in one export.
2. Filter by **refund date** for the range above. If the processor only exposes the charge date, export both dates and count rows by refund date.
3. Read the processor's record count for that filter. Fetch **every page** until you have that many rows or the API says there are no more.
4. Compare rows exported to the processor's count. If they differ, **stop** and report the two numbers. Do not pad, deduplicate silently, or "fix" the difference.
5. Include refunds whose status is settled or succeeded. List pending, failed and cancelled refunds on a second sheet with counts and amounts — do not add them to the total.
6. Keep each row in its **original currency**. Report a subtotal per currency. Never sum across currencies without a rate the owner has supplied, and state the rate and its date if you use one.
7. Reconcile: the processor shows its own total for the same filter. Compare it to your sum. If they differ by any amount, **stop** and report the difference rather than writing it off to rounding.
8. Save to a **new** file named `refunds-YYYY-MM`, never overwriting an existing one. Tell the owner the file name and where it is.

## Columns

`refund_id, refund_date, charge_id, customer_ref, amount, currency, status, processor_fee`

Example row (invented values, not a real customer):

`RF-00481, 2025-06-14, CH-77120, CUST-1042, -48.00, USD, settled, -1.69`

State the sign convention in the header: negative means money returned to the customer.

## Never

- **Never put the API key in the sheet, the file name, a message, or a report.** Read it from the owner's secret store or environment at run time. If you can't find it, ask — don't go looking for one in old messages.
- Never include a full card number. Last four only, and only if the owner asked for it; most refund reports don't need card data at all. Use the customer reference where one exists.
- Never send the finished sheet to anyone but the owner, and never to an address you weren't given.
- Never report a total you could not reconcile.

## Stop and ask when

- The month or time zone is ambiguous.
- You can't tell whether you're in live or test mode.
- The exported row count or the total doesn't match the processor's figure.
- Refunds span more than one currency and no rate was given.
- A refund's amount is larger than its original charge, or a refund appears more than once for the same charge.
```

# Monthly Refunds to Spreadsheet

Export every refund created in the previous calendar month from a payment
processor into a spreadsheet, with a reconciliation check against the
processor's own totals.

## Data and secrets — read this first

This skill is published in a public catalog. Everything in it must be safe
to share with other companies.

- **Never hardcode an API key, token, or customer data** in this file, in a
  prompt, in a sheet title, in a filename, in a chat message, or in a commit.
  Read credentials at runtime from an environment variable or secret manager.
- **Never export full card numbers, CVCs, or government IDs.** Last-4 and card
  brand only.
- **Every example below is fictional.** The customer name, card digits, IDs,
  and key are placeholders. Do not replace them with real values in this file;
  substitute at runtime.
- **If a key is ever exposed** — pasted into a doc, ticket, chat, or repo —
  treat it as compromised: revoke and rotate it in the processor dashboard,
  then review logs for unexpected use.

## Configuration

Environment variables (or equivalents from your secret store):

| Variable | Purpose | Example (placeholder) |
|---|---|---|
| `PAYMENT_PROCESSOR_BASE_URL` | API base URL | `https://api.example-processor.com/v1` |
| `PAYMENT_PROCESSOR_API_KEY` | Read-only key scoped to refunds | `pp_test_0000000000000000` |
| `REPORT_TIMEZONE` | Timezone for "last month" | `America/New_York` |

Use a **read-only key scoped to refunds**, and prefer a sandbox/test key
until the workflow is verified. Never use a live key in an example or a demo.

## Step 1 — Compute the window

"Last month" means the previous calendar month in `REPORT_TIMEZONE`, as a
half-open interval `[start, end)`.

```
start = first instant of last month, 00:00:00 local
end   = first instant of this month,  00:00:00 local
```

Convert both to UTC for the API call. Watch for DST: the offset at `start`
and at `end` may differ.

Example: if today is 2025-04-03 and `REPORT_TIMEZONE=America/New_York`:

```
start = 2025-03-01T00:00:00-05:00  ->  2025-03-01T05:00:00Z
end   = 2025-04-01T00:00:00-04:00  ->  2025-04-01T04:00:00Z
```

## Step 2 — Fetch refunds

```
GET {PAYMENT_PROCESSOR_BASE_URL}/refunds
    ?created[gte]=2025-03-01T05:00:00Z
    &created[lt]=2025-04-01T04:00:00Z
    &limit=100
Authorization: Bearer ${PAYMENT_PROCESSOR_API_KEY}
```

- Paginate until the response has no next cursor / `has_more` is false.
- Retry on HTTP 429 and 5xx with exponential backoff (1s, 2s, 4s, 8s),
  honoring `Retry-After`. Cap at 5 attempts, then stop and report the error
  rather than silently truncating.
- Record the total count the API reports, for verification in Step 5.

## Step 3 — Normalize rows

One row per refund. Columns, in this order:

| Column | Notes |
|---|---|
| `refund_id` | Processor's refund ID |
| `created_at_utc` | ISO 8601, UTC |
| `status` | e.g. `succeeded`, `pending`, `failed` |
| `amount` | Decimal, from minor units (cents / 100) |
| `currency` | ISO 4217 |
| `payment_id` | Charge or payment intent the refund belongs to |
| `customer_id` | Processor customer ID |
| `customer_name` | Display name only |
| `card_brand` | e.g. `Visa` |
| `card_last4` | Last 4 only — never the full number |
| `reason` | Processor's reason code |
| `description` | Free text, if present |
| `livemode` | `true`/`false` — keep this so sandbox rows are never mixed with live rows |

Do not add full PAN, CVC, expiry, or full billing address.

## Step 4 — Write the spreadsheet

- Write a CSV first: `refunds_YYYY-MM.csv` (e.g. `refunds_2025-03.csv`),
  header row, no merged cells, dates in ISO 8601.
- To place it in Google Sheets: create or replace a tab named
  `Refunds YYYY-MM`, write the header, then append rows in batches of 500.
- Do not put customer names in the filename or the tab name.

## Step 5 — Verify before reporting

- Row count equals the API's reported total for the window.
- `sum(amount)` per currency equals the processor's reported refund total for
  the window. If they differ, stop and investigate; do not report a total.
- No `failed` rows unless the user asked for them.
- Spot-check 3 refund IDs with `GET /refunds/{id}` and confirm they match.
- Confirm no `livemode=false` rows are mixed in if the user asked for live data.

Report line:

> Pulled **N** refunds for **March 2025**. Total: **$X.XX** (and any other
> currencies separately). Duplicates: **0**. Source: processor API, verified
> against processor totals.

## Worked example (fictional data)

Config:

```
PAYMENT_PROCESSOR_BASE_URL=https://api.example-processor.com/v1
PAYMENT_PROCESSOR_API_KEY=pp_test_0000000000000000
REPORT_TIMEZONE=America/New_York
```

| `rf_example_001` | 2025-03-04T15:22:10Z | succeeded | 24.00 | USD | Example Customer | Visa | 0000 | false |
| `rf_example_002` | 2025-03-19T09:01:44Z | succeeded | 9.50 | USD | Sample Buyer | Mastercard | 1111 | false |

Verification output:

> Pulled **2** refunds for **March 2025**. Total: **$33.50 USD**.
> Duplicates: **0**. Source: processor API, verified against processor totals.

## Failure modes and what to do

| Symptom | Action |
|---|---|
| 401 / 403 | Key missing, expired, or lacks refunds scope. Do not retry blindly; report to the user. |
| 429 persisted after 5 retries | Stop. Report rows fetched so far as partial; do not present as complete. |
| Row count ≠ API total | Re-run pagination from the start; check for a second timezone conversion. |
| Sum mismatch | Do not report a total. Flag for human review. |

# Vendor Invoice Reconciliation & Payment Terms

## Core rule
Two jobs, one wall between them. Reconciliation is a control: it establishes what is owed. Negotiation is commercial: it sets when it gets paid. The agent may do both, but must never trade one for the other. A discrepancy is never waived or "smoothed over" in exchange for better terms — that is how overbilling gets laundered. If a vendor offers terms in return for dropping a variance, decline and escalate.

## Part 1 — Reconcile
Match every invoice three ways: purchase order → receipt/acceptance → invoice. Line by line: quantity, unit price, extended price, freight, tax, discount, currency.

Hold payment and flag on:
- Price above PO or contracted price, or any variance over [tolerance]
- Quantity billed greater than quantity received
- Duplicate: same vendor + invoice number, or same amount within 45 days
- Missing PO, missing receipt, or unapproved PO
- Tax or freight not on the PO
- Any change to bank details — hold and verify by phone to a known number, never by reply email

Never pay an unmatched invoice. Never edit a vendor invoice; record the variance instead.

Record one line per invoice: vendor · invoice no. · date · amount · PO · match status · variance amount · reason code · action (approve / hold / dispute) · approver.

Dispute in writing, every time: invoice number, PO number, the exact variance, the amount you will pay, and a response deadline.

## Part 2 — Negotiate terms
Know before you ask: current terms, monthly invoice volume, actual days-to-pay, on-time rate, sole-source status.

Ask for, in order:
1. Early-pay discount — target 2/10 net 30
2. Longer net terms — Net 45/60 at no price increase
3. Removal of late fees, cleaner remittance
4. Consolidated or volume billing

Trade only what you own: payment timing, consolidation, forecast visibility, fast dispute handling. Never trade accuracy, and never promise volume you cannot see.

Authority: [amount] and term changes up to [days]. Beyond that, get owner approval before agreeing. Log every agreed change with its effective date.

## Escalate to owner
Bank detail change · variance over [threshold] · vendor refuses to correct · terms offered in exchange for a discrepancy · sole-source vendor · any pressure or urgency.
```

```markdown
---
name: vendor-invoice-reconciliation
description: Reconciles a vendor invoice against its purchase order and receipt, records the outcome, and flags exceptions for a person. Use when an invoice arrives or a batch must be cleared before payment.
---

# Reconcile a Vendor Invoice

**The mistake this fixes:** an invoice marked matched because the totals agree while the line items don't, and a duplicate paid because its number was punctuated differently. Both surface at audit, months later.

**You need:** the invoice, its purchase order, the receipt (goods or service), and the vendor record. Missing any one of these stops the job at step 2.

1. Read the invoice and record it exactly: vendor, invoice number as printed, date, currency, total. Do not reformat or "tidy" the number.

2. Check for a duplicate before matching. Search the system for the same vendor with the same number (ignore spaces, punctuation, leading zeros), or the same amount within 30 days. If a candidate appears, stop and ask — do not decide it is or isn't a duplicate.

3. Match to the purchase order. A match requires all of: same vendor, a PO number or a documented reference, same currency, and a total inside the tolerance the owner has set. If no tolerance has been set, ask for one; do not choose your own.

4. Compare line by line, not just the total. For each line check quantity invoiced against quantity received, unit price against PO price, and description against what was ordered. A total that agrees while a line does not is still an exception — name the line.

5. Handle differences; never smooth them. Price above PO: exception. Quantity above receipt: exception. Freight or rounding inside tolerance: record it and note it. Never edit the invoice, the PO or the receipt to force agreement, and never split an invoice to slip under an approval limit.

6. Recheck the arithmetic. Quantity × unit price on every line, lines summed to the subtotal, tax applied to the right base, credits deducted. An invoice can be internally wrong and still match the PO.

7. Record the outcome in the accounting system: matched or exception, a reason code, and the figures you compared. Do not approve, post, schedule payment, or touch the vendor's bank details.

8. Stop and ask the owner when: there is no PO or no receipt; a duplicate is possible; price or quantity exceeds the PO or receipt; the vendor is unknown or its bank details differ from the vendor record; the difference is outside tolerance; the invoice exceeds the approval limit you were given; the currency or tax cannot be verified. State what you checked, what did not agree, and which document you need.

9. Never: approve or pay an invoice, alter a source document, delete a record, or agree a change with the vendor. A vendor conversation about price, credit or timing is a negotiation — hand it to whoever owns the vendor relationship.

Work one invoice at a time and finish step 7 before starting the next, even in a batch.
```

---

```markdown
---
name: guest-time-zone-booking
description: Books a meeting at the guest's local time, not the owner's, and states both zones in the invite. Use whenever an invite goes to someone outside the owner's organization or time zone.
---

# Book the Guest's Time, Not Your Own

Last month 9 of 20 invites to outside guests were off by one to three hours, and two guests missed their calls. The cause is always the same: a time worked out in the owner's zone and sent as if it were the guest's. These are the checks that catch it before the invite goes out.

## 1. Find the guest's zone before you open the calendar
Read the guest's own words first: a signature with a city, a phone number with a country code, "I'm in Nairobi this week". Check the thread, the CRM record and the guest's company contact page.

Country is not a zone — the United States, Canada, Australia, Brazil and Russia each span several; if you only know the country, you don't know the zone. Abbreviations are not zones either: IST is India, Ireland or Israel; CST is US Central, China or Cuba. Write the city or the full zone name.

## 2. If you can't establish it, stop and ask
Ask the guest before sending: "Which time zone should I use for our call?" Do not send the invite and wait to be corrected.

Also stop and ask when the only workable slot falls outside 08:00–18:00 in the guest's zone, when the guest names a time with no zone and you can't tell which one they mean, or when the date is within three days of a daylight-saving change in either zone.

## 3. Convert through UTC, then check by a second route
Convert guest local → UTC → owner local, and write both numbers down. Then check by a different method: a world clock, the calendar's zone preview, or counting back from the guest's stated time. If the two answers differ, you have found the bug — do not pick the one you prefer.

Do not round. Half-hour and three-quarter-hour zones (5:30, 5:45, 8:45) are where the errors hide.

## 4. Put both zones in the invite
The invite body carries the time twice, guest first:

"Tuesday 14 April, 15:00–15:30 WEST (your time) / 16:00–16:30 SAST (my time). Please reply if either is wrong."

Give the day and the date. A guest who reads only "3pm" in another zone has no way to check it.

## 5. Read the saved event back
After saving, open the event and read the time the calendar shows for the guest's zone, not the owner's. If your calendar stores a single time zone for the event, that is fine — what matters is that the guest's own local time appears in the invite they receive.

## Never
- Never send an invite whose only stated time is in the owner's zone.
- Never change a time the guest has already confirmed in their own words in their own zone.
- Never write a zone abbreviation you haven't tied to a city.

## Example
Nadia Okafor of Brightwater Freight writes from Lagos asking for a 30-minute call on Thursday morning; the owner is in Berlin. Thursday 10:00 WAT = 09:00 UTC = 11:00 CEST. The invite reads: "Thursday 12 June, 10:00–10:30 WAT (your time) / 11:00–11:30 CEST (my time)."
```

```markdown
---
name: guest-time-zone-meetings
description: Book meetings with outside guests in the guest's time zone and show both the guest's and owner's local times in every invite. Use when proposing, booking, rescheduling, or confirming a meeting with someone outside the owner's organization.
---

# Book Meetings in the Guest's Time Zone

**The failure this fixes:** agents book outside-guest meetings in the owner's or calendar's time zone. The guest arrives at the wrong hour. Last month this happened on 9 of 20 outside invites; two customers missed calls.

## 1. Find the guest's time zone before you propose a time
- Read the guest's latest message and signature for a city or zone. Check earlier messages in the thread and the contact record.
- Ask which time zone the guest will be in **on the meeting date**, not just where they live. A guest may be travelling.
- Record a named zone: "Europe/Berlin", "US Eastern", "Asia/Kolkata". A city plus country is acceptable. Do not use an abbreviation alone: "CST" could mean US Central or China Standard.
- If the guest gives a time but no zone, do not guess from their country, area code or the owner's location. Ask: "To make sure I have this right, are you on Central Time in Chicago?"
- If two sources disagree, stop and ask the guest to confirm. Do not send the invite.

## 2. Convert for the meeting date, not today
- Check the daylight-saving rules in both zones for the date of the meeting. An offset that is correct today may be wrong next month.
- If the meeting falls near a clock change, check the date in both zones. The changes may happen on different dates.
- Check the date as well as the hour. A morning meeting in Sydney can be the previous afternoon in New York.
- For a recurring meeting, check the first and last occurrence across any clock change.

## 3. Put both local times in the invite
Use this pattern in the invite body, with the guest's time first.

Example (test values):
> Proposed: Tuesday 14 May, 10:00–10:30 your time (Europe/Berlin); 16:00–16:30 the owner's time (US Eastern).

- Name both zones. Never write "10:00" alone.
- In the calendar, enter the event so the saved start and end are the correct instant. If the calendar has a time-zone field, set it to the guest's zone; otherwise enter the equivalent in the calendar's zone.
- Save, reopen the event, and check the displayed time and zone. If the calendar shows a different time from your invite text, stop and fix it before sending.
- If the calendar can show a second time zone, use it to check the guest's view.
- Send the invite only after the guest's zone, both local times and the date match.

## 4. Stop and ask when
- the guest's zone is missing or ambiguous;
- the guest's city is in a country with more than one zone and you cannot tell which;
- the guest says "morning" or "afternoon" without a zone;
- the meeting is within two days of a daylight-saving change and you are unsure;
- the calendar shows a different time after saving;
- the guest's stated time conflicts with the time you calculated.

Ask one direct question and wait. Do not book a "best guess" while you wait.

## 5. Never
- Never assume the guest is in the owner's time zone or the calendar's default zone.
- Never use a bare time-zone abbreviation as the only zone label.
- Never silently change a time the guest wrote. Say what you see: "You wrote 3pm; I have that as 3pm US Eastern. Is that right?"
- Never send an outside invite with only one zone shown.
- Never leave an old invite active after a time-zone correction. Update or cancel it and tell the guest.
```

> screenshot or a chat message.

## What you produce

1. A spreadsheet tab named `refunds_YYYY-MM` (e.g. `refunds_2025-02`).
2. One row per refund created in that calendar month.
3. A short reconciliation summary: row count, refund count, total amount, and a
   pass/fail against the processor's own total for the same period.

## Before you start

- **Credentials:** an API key with read-only permission on refunds and charges.
  It must live in an environment variable or secret manager, never in code, a
  spreadsheet cell, or a document. This skill assumes `PAYMENTS_API_KEY`.
- **Date rules:** confirm with the requester which month and which timezone counts
  as "last month". If nobody says otherwise, use the company's accounting timezone,
  not your laptop's.
- **Spreadsheet access:** permission to create a file and append rows.
- **Scope:** refunds only. Do not pull full card numbers, CVCs, or expiry dates —
  the processor will not give them to you, and you should not want them.

## Step 1 — Pin the date range

Compute the range once, in the processor's timezone, as a half-open interval
`[start, end)` in ISO 8601 UTC. Half-open means the first instant of the month is
included and the first instant of the next month is excluded — this is what stops
the boundary day being counted twice or dropped.

Example: if today is 2025-03-04 and the requester means February 2025:

- `start = 2025-02-01T00:00:00Z`
- `end   = 2025-03-01T00:00:00Z`

Write both values into a cell or a note in the output so the range is auditable.

Common failure: using local midnight. A team in UTC-5 asking for February will
miss the first five hours of 1 February and pick up five hours of 1 March.

## Step 2 — Authenticate

Read the key from the environment at runtime:

```bash
# The value is never printed. Never echo it.
: "${PAYMENTS_API_KEY:?set PAYMENTS_API_KEY in your environment or secret manager}"
```

Send it as a bearer token:

```
Authorization: Bearer $PAYMENTS_API_KEY
```

Rules:

- **Never** log the key, paste it into a cell, a chat, a ticket, or a screenshot.
- **Never** commit it. If you find one committed, treat it as leaked and rotate it.
- Check the prefix before you run anything that writes: test-mode keys are for
  rehearsals, live keys are for the real export. If you're unsure which you have,
  ask before running.
- Use a read-only key. An export has no reason to be able to create refunds.

## Step 3 — Page through the refunds

Request refunds filtered by creation time, newest first, in pages:

```
GET /v1/refunds
  ?created[gte]=2025-02-01T00:00:00Z
  &created[lt]=2025-03-01T00:00:00Z
  &limit=100
  &starting_after=<last_id_from_previous_page>
```

Loop until the response returns an empty `data` array or no `has_more`. Do not
assume one page is the whole month — the default page size is far smaller than a
busy month's refunds, and a truncated export that looks complete is the worst
outcome here.

Handle the ordinary failure modes:

- **429 / rate limited:** wait and retry with exponential backoff (start ~1s,
  double, cap at ~60s, give up after 5 attempts).
- **5xx:** same backoff; these are transient.
- **4xx other than 429:** stop and report. Do not retry a malformed request.
- **Timeouts:** retry the same page with the same cursor; do not restart the whole
  export.

A single refund object looks like this (fictional):

```json
{
  "id": "re_EXAMPLE_0001",
  "object": "refund",
  "amount": 4200,
  "currency": "usd",
  "status": "succeeded",
  "created": 1738454400,
  "charge": "ch_EXAMPLE_0001",
  "reason": "requested_by_customer",
  "payment_method_details": {
    "card": { "brand": "visa", "last4": "0000" }
  },
  "customer": { "id": "cus_EXAMPLE_01", "name": "Sample Customer" }
}
```

Note what you get and what you don't: `last4` only, no full number. Keep it that way.

## Step 4 — Map to columns

Create the header row exactly once, then append:

| Column | Source | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `refund_id` | `id` | unique key for de-duplication |
| `created_at_utc` | `created` | convert epoch seconds to ISO 8601 UTC |
| `customer_id` | `customer.id` | prefer the ID over the name |
| `customer_name` | `customer.name` | optional; include only if policy allows |
| `card_brand` | `payment_method_details.card.brand` | |
| `card_last4` | `payment_method_details.card.last4` | last four only, never more |
| `amount_minor` | `amount` | integer, smallest currency unit |
| `amount_display` | derived | `amount_minor / 100`, formatted |
| `currency` | `currency` | |
| `status` | `status` | `succeeded`, `pending`, `failed`, … |
| `reason` | `reason` | may be empty |
| `charge_id` | `charge` | for cross-checking |

Mapping rules:

- **Amounts stay integers** in minor units in their own column. Never store money
  as a float; rounding will bite you at reconciliation.
- **De-duplicate on `refund_id`** before appending, in case a retry re-fetches a page.
- **Do not** add columns for full card number, expiry, CVC, billing address, or
  anything else the task didn't ask for.

## Step 5 — Write to the spreadsheet

1. Create the file or tab and name it `refunds_YYYY-MM`.
2. Write the header row, freeze it, and set the date and currency formats.
3. Append rows in batches of a few hundred — not one call per row.
4. Leave a `Notes` area with the date range, the run timestamp, and the mode
   (test or live).

Share the finished file with named people only. A "anyone with the link" export of
customer payment data is how these end up outside the company.

## Step 6 — Reconcile before you hand it over

Do all three checks and write the results into the summary:

1. **Totals:** sum of `amount_minor` for `status = succeeded` in the sheet must
   equal the processor's own refund total for the same range. Tolerance is zero
   minor units.
2. **Counts:** number of rows must equal the number of refund objects returned across
   all pages. If they differ, you have a pagination or de-duplication bug.
3. **Spot check:** open the processor dashboard for the same month, sort refunds by
   amount, and confirm the largest two or three appear in the sheet with the same
   values.

Decide explicitly what the requester wants done with `pending` and `failed` refunds.
Default: keep them in the sheet with their status, exclude them from the total, and
say so.

Worked example of the summary (fictional):

```
Range:        2025-02-01T00:00:00Z to 2025-03-01T00:00:00Z
Rows:         3 (2 succeeded, 1 failed)
Total:        USD 82.00 succeeded  (4,200 + 4,000 minor units)
Processor:    USD 82.00
Result:       PASS — counts and totals match
```

And the matching sheet rows:

| refund_id | created_at_utc | customer_id | card_brand | card_last4 | amount_minor | status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| re_EXAMPLE_0001 | 2025-02-02T09:15:00Z | cus_EXAMPLE_01 | visa | 0000 | 4200 | succeeded |
| re_EXAMPLE_0002 | 2025-02-14T16:40:00Z | cus_EXAMPLE_02 | mastercard | 0000 | 4000 | succeeded |
| re_EXAMPLE_0003 | 2025-02-27T11:02:00Z | cus_EXAMPLE_01 | visa | 0000 | 1500 | failed |

## Step 7 — Report

Give the requester: the file link, the date range, the row count, the succeeded
total, and the reconciliation result. Log the API request IDs so a failed run can be
traced, but never log request bodies, keys, or customer details.

## Privacy and safety checklist

Before you finish, confirm:

- [ ] No API key appears in the sheet, the code, the logs, the chat, or the ticket.
- [ ] No full card number, expiry or CVC anywhere — `last4` at most.
- [ ] Customer names included only if the requester needs them; IDs otherwise.
- [ ] File shared with named people, not "anyone with the link".
- [ ] Raw exports deleted after reconciliation per the retention policy.
- [ ] If a key was exposed, it has been rotated, not just deleted from the message.

## Common mistakes

- Off-by-one on the month boundary because of local time instead of UTC.
- Stopping after the first page.
- Counting `pending` or `failed` refunds in the total.
- Storing money as a float.
- Re-running the export and duplicating rows instead of de-duplicating on `refund_id`.
- Pasting the key "just for a second" into a cell or a chat.
- Running the real export against a live key when a test run was intended.

name: pulling-monthly-refunds
description: "Export last month's refunds from the payment processor into a spreadsheet. Use when a task asks for a monthly refund report, a refund reconciliation, or refund totals for a period."

# Pulling Last Month's Refunds into a Spreadsheet

## Before you start
1. Get a **read-only** API key for the processor from the team's secret manager. Never paste a key into a document, a chat message, a script, or this file. Load it at run time from an environment variable, e.g. `PROCESSOR_API_KEY`.
2. Confirm the account's timezone. "Last month" means the first moment to the last moment of the previous calendar month **in that timezone**.
3. Confirm the processor's base URL and API version, e.g. `https://api.example-processor.com/v1`. Store it in `PROCESSOR_BASE_URL`.
4. Confirm how the processor wants date filters and pagination — parameter names differ. The examples below use `created[gte]`, `created[lte]`, `limit`, and a `next_cursor`; adapt to your processor's docs.

## Step 1: Work out the date range
1. Set `start` to the first day of last month at 00:00:00.
2. Set `end` to the last day of last month at 23:59:59.
3. Convert both to Unix timestamps in UTC.
4. Write the range down before you call anything. Example: if today is 2026-03-04 and the account is on UTC, last month is `2026-02-01T00:00:00Z` (1769904000) through `2026-02-28T23:59:59Z` (1772323199).

## Step 2: Fetch refunds, page by page
1. Call the refunds list endpoint:
   `GET {PROCESSOR_BASE_URL}/refunds?created[gte]={start}&created[lte]={end}&limit=100`
2. Send the key in the header, never in the URL:
   `Authorization: Bearer $PROCESSOR_API_KEY`
3. Read `has_more` (or `next_cursor`) from the response and keep calling until there are no more pages. **Do not assume the first page is everything.**
4. Handle errors explicitly:
   - `401` — key missing, wrong, or revoked. Stop; do not retry with a different key.
   - `429` — rate limited. Back off (e.g. 1s, 2s, 4s…) and retry.
   - `5xx` — retry with exponential backoff, then stop and report.
5. Log only refund IDs, amounts, and status codes. Never log the key, full response bodies with personal data, or card numbers.

## Step 3: Shape the rows
Use these columns, in this order:
1. `refund_id`
2. `created_at` — ISO 8601, UTC
3. `customer_name`
4. `customer_id`
5. `card_last4`
6. `amount` — converted from minor units (cents) to major units
7. `currency`
8. `status`
9. `payment_id`
10. `reason`

Include every refund returned for the period. Put `status` in its own column rather than silently dropping pending or failed ones — then totals are easy to explain.

## Step 4: Write the spreadsheet
1. Write a CSV named `refunds-YYYY-MM.csv` (e.g. `refunds-2026-02.csv`).
2. Quote any field containing a comma or a quote.
3. Add a totals block below the data: count of refunds and sum of `amount`, per currency. Never add different currencies together.

## Step 5: Check the numbers before you send it
1. Compare the count and the per-currency totals against the processor dashboard for the same month. They should match to the cent.
2. Spot-check three refunds by opening them in the dashboard and comparing every column.
3. If they don't match, check these first, in order: pagination (did you read every page?), timezone (is "last month" off by a day?), and units (cents treated as dollars).

## Example
Today is 2026-03-04, account timezone UTC. Last month is February 2026.

Request:
```
GET https://api.example-processor.com/v1/refunds?created[gte]=1769904000&created[lte]=1772323199&limit=100
Authorization: Bearer $PROCESSOR_API_KEY
```
(The key is loaded from the secret manager at run time. It is never written into the skill, the script, or the output.)

One refund object from the response (illustrative values, not a real customer):
```json
{
  "id": "re_00000000000000",
  "created": 1770000000,
  "amount": 2500,
  "currency": "usd",
  "status": "succeeded",
  "payment": "pay_00000000000000",
  "customer": { "id": "cus_00000000000000", "name": "Example Customer" },
  "payment_method_details": { "card": { "last4": "0000" } },
  "reason": "requested_by_customer"
}
```

Resulting spreadsheet row:
```
re_00000000000000, 2026-02-02T02:40:00Z, Example Customer, cus_00000000000000, 0000, 25.00, usd, succeeded, pay_00000000000000, requested_by_customer
```

Totals block:
```
refund_count,currency,total_amount
1,usd,25.00
```

## Secrets and personal data
1. Keys: read-only, stored in the secret manager, loaded from an environment variable, never committed, never printed, never pasted into a document. Rotate immediately if one is exposed.
2. A public skill file must never contain a real customer's name, card digits, email, or address. Use made-up placeholders that keep the same shape.
3. The output spreadsheet contains customer data. Save it only to the approved drive, share it only with people who need it, and delete it when the reconciliation is done.

## Common mistakes
1. Reading only page 1 and reporting a total that's too low.
2. Using the local timezone instead of the account's timezone.
3. Treating cents as dollars.
4. Adding different currencies together.
5. Dropping pending or failed refunds without saying so.
6. Hardcoding the API key "just for testing."

```markdown
---
name: reconcile-monthly-refunds
description: Pulls one month of refunds from the payment processor into a spreadsheet and ties the total to the processor's own monthly report. Use when the owner asks for last month's refunds, a refunds export, or a refund total for a period.
---

# Reconcile Monthly Refunds

**The failure this prevents:** the refunds sheet totals a different amount than the
processor's own monthly report. The owner passes the wrong figure to their
bookkeeper and it comes back weeks later. The usual causes are a date window read
in the wrong time zone, a pull that stopped at the first page of results, and
non-refund transactions counted as refunds.

## 1. Pin the month and the date field
- "Last month" means the previous full calendar month in the business's time zone —
  not yours, not UTC. Write the range as two ISO dates (for example 2025-04-01 to
  2025-04-30) and state the time zone.
- Ask whether the report should use the date the refund was created or the date it
  settled. These differ, sometimes by days, and the processor's monthly summary
  uses one of them. If the owner has not said which, ask before pulling. Record the
  choice on the sheet.

## 2. Pull the full export, not what is on screen
- Use the processor's downloadable report or its paginated list, not a total read
  off a dashboard.
- Follow pagination to the last page. Count the records you received.
- Compare your count with the count on the processor's monthly summary. If yours is
  lower, you stopped early or the filter is wrong. Fix it; never hand over a partial
  pull as if it were the month.

## 3. Keep refunds only
- Include refunds. Exclude voids, chargebacks, reversals, disputes, and failed or
  pending refunds.
- If the export mixes them, filter on transaction type and status. List everything
  excluded on a second tab marked "not counted", so the owner can see it was seen
  and left out.

## 4. Columns and formatting
One row per refund: refund date (ISO yyyy-mm-dd), refund id, original payment id,
amount, currency, status, and reason if the processor gives one.
- Amounts as numbers with two decimals, not text. No merged cells, no subtotal rows
  inside the data.
- Totals go on their own tab, or below the data after a blank row.
- Never put a full card number, security code or expiry date in the sheet, the file
  name, a chat message or this skill. Last four only if the owner asks for it, and
  only alongside the processor's own transaction id.

## 5. Credentials
Read the API key from the environment or secret store the owner has set up, by name.
Never write the key into a script, a spreadsheet, a sheet name, a chat message or a
report. If you cannot find it, stop and ask. Never use a key that was pasted into a
message to you.

## 6. Reconcile before handing over
- Compare your total per currency with the processor's monthly refund total for the
  same range and the same date field.
- Put both numbers and the difference in the cover note. A difference of zero is the
  pass condition.
- If the owner cannot give you the processor's monthly figure, say so and mark the
  total "unreconciled". Do not call it verified.
- Do not make it balance by editing rows, dropping outliers or rounding. If it does
  not tie after one honest re-check, report the gap and stop.
- Never add currencies together. One total per currency.

## 7. What the owner receives
A spreadsheet with a data tab, a "not counted" tab and a totals tab; plus a short
cover note: month and time zone, date field used, record count, total per currency,
the processor's figure, and the difference.

## 8. Stop and ask when
- the month or the time zone is unclear;
- the date field matters and nobody has chosen one;
- the export spans more than one account or currency and you do not know how the
  owner wants them split;
- the totals do not tie after one honest re-check;
- the task needs a permission or scope you do not have.

## 9. Never
- Never present a partial, filtered or sampled pull as the month's refunds.
- Never invent or adjust a row to close a gap.
- Never include card data or an API key.
- Never decide whether a refund is owed, how it is taxed, or who is liable. That is
  for the owner or their accountant.

**Example (invented test values, not real people or accounts):** Meridian Row Ltd
asks for March 2025 refunds, settled date, Europe/London. The pull returns 14
refunds totalling 812.40 EUR across three pages; the processor's March summary shows
812.40 EUR. The cover note states 14 records, 812.40 EUR, difference 0.00. One
refund, RF-1042 for customer Dana Whitfield, card ending 0000, was still pending and
sits on the "not counted" tab.
```

description: >

# Scheduling across time zones

## Why this skill exists

Agents default to the owner's calendar time zone. The owner's calendar is the
agent's whole world, so "2pm" quietly means "2pm where my owner is." Last month
9 of 20 invites to outside guests were off by one to three hours and two
customers missed calls. Every one of those was avoidable: the agent was never
told the guest's zone and filled the gap with a guess.

**The rule: a time zone is a fact you are given, never a fact you infer.**

If you do not know the guest's zone, you do not know the time. Say so.

---

## The No-Guess Gate

Do not create, send, or verbally confirm a calendar invite for an outside guest
until the guest's zone comes from one of exactly three sources:

| # | Allowed source | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **The guest stated it** | "I'm in Berlin" / "Pacific time" / a city + country |
| 2 | **A previously confirmed event or contact record** | CRM field `timezone: Europe/Berlin`, set when source 1 confirmed it |
| 3 | **The guest picked it themselves** | They booked through a scheduling link that renders in their browser's zone |

**Never** derive a zone from:

- the owner's calendar default or the calendar API's default
- an email domain (`.de`, `.co.uk`, `.in` prove nothing about where someone is)
- a phone country code or area code
- the language the guest writes in
- the time zone of the last meeting, if the guest has since travelled
- a time zone abbreviation (see below)

If none of the three sources is available, use the **Ask First** script and
stop. Do not send a "provisional" invite as a way of asking.

---

## Procedure

### Step 1 — Resolve the guest's zone

Ask for a **city and country**, not a zone name and not an offset. Cities survive
DST; offsets and abbreviations do not.

> **Ask First (guest zone unknown):**
> Hi [Name] — happy to get this on the calendar. Before I do: which city and
> country will you be in on [date]? I book meetings in the guest's local time and
> I'd rather ask than guess.

If the guest is a stranger, a prospect, or anyone you have no relationship with,
the better move is often a booking link — they select a slot in their own zone
and the ambiguity disappears. Offer the link before offering a time.

### Step 2 — Store the zone as an IANA identifier

Convert the answer to an IANA name (`Europe/Berlin`, `America/Chicago`,
`Asia/Kolkata`) and write it to the contact record in the CRM alongside the
meeting. Use IANA names everywhere internally. `Europe/Berlin` encodes the DST
rules; `+01:00` and `CET` do not.

If the guest gives a city that spans zones (e.g. "Portland" — Oregon vs. Maine),
ask once which one. One question is cheaper than one missed call.

### Step 3 — Compute the instant, not the hour

Work in UTC. Convert owner-local → UTC → guest-local using the tz database for
that specific date. Never add or subtract a fixed number of hours from a
remembered offset.

```
guest_local = utc_instant.in_zone(guest_tz)
owner_local = utc_instant.in_zone(owner_tz)
```

The stored value is the UTC instant. Both local renderings are derived from it.

### Step 4 — Apply the two-clock rule

Anything a human reads states the time **twice, with city labels**, plus the
day-of-week, because a six-hour gap crosses midnight in one direction.

> **Proposal:**
> Does Tuesday, 11 March at 9:00 a.m. Chicago time work? That's 15:00 the same
> day in Berlin.
> — or, if the days differ —
> Does Monday, 10 March at 6:00 p.m. Chicago time work? That's 08:00 Tuesday
> in Tokyo.

Never write a bare "2pm." Never write "2pm EST" to a guest — write
"2:00 p.m. New York time."

### Step 5 — Write the event so the provider cannot re-interpret it

Set the absolute offset **and** the IANA zone. Providers that receive an offset
without a zone may re-render the event in the calendar owner's zone on save.

**Google Calendar API**
```json
"start": { "dateTime": "2025-03-11T09:00:00-05:00", "timeZone": "America/Chicago" },
"end":   { "dateTime": "2025-03-11T09:30:00-05:00", "timeZone": "America/Chicago" }
```
The `timeZone` field governs recurrence expansion — get it wrong and every
future occurrence drifts at the next DST change.

**Microsoft Graph / Outlook**
Send UTC and say so. Windows time zone names (`Central Standard Time`) are
DST-ambiguous by construction.
```json
"start": { "dateTime": "2025-03-11T14:00:00", "timeZone": "UTC" },
"end":   { "dateTime": "2025-03-11T14:30:00", "timeZone": "UTC" }
```

**CalDAV / Apple Calendar**
```
DTSTART;TZID=America/Chicago:20250311T090000
DTEND;TZID=America/Chicago:20250311T093000
```
Include the matching `VTIMEZONE` component.

**Calendly / Cal.com / other booking tools**
Do not override the invitee's detected zone, and do not "correct" a slot the
guest picked. Their browser already did the conversion correctly.

### Step 6 — Put both clocks in the invite body

```
When:  Tuesday, 11 March 2025
       9:00 – 9:30 a.m.  Chicago (CDT)
       15:00 – 15:30     Berlin (CET)

Joining: [link]  |  Dial-in: [number] (local numbers listed in the invite)
```

Add the guest's city to the event location or description. It is the cheapest
possible defence against a future agent reading the event and re-guessing.

### Step 7 — Verify by reading back

After writing, fetch the event and re-render both zones from the stored value.
Confirm:

- [ ] The UTC instant read back equals the UTC instant you intended.
- [ ] The guest-side rendering matches what you told the guest in writing.
- [ ] The `timeZone` field is the IANA name, not an offset and not a Windows name.
- [ ] For recurring events, the *next* occurrence after any DST transition still
      lands on the intended local hour.
- [ ] The dial-in number's country matches the guest's country, or a local number
      is listed.

If any check fails, fix it before the confirmation goes out. A wrong invite that
was never sent costs nothing.

### Step 8 — Confirm ambiguous replies

A guest replying "2pm works" has not told you whose 2pm. Close the loop in one
line:

> Just to be sure — 2:00 p.m. your time in Berlin, which is 8:00 a.m. here in
> Chicago. I'll send the invite on that basis.

---

## Time zone abbreviations are not time zones

Refuse to act on an abbreviation alone. Ask, or use the city.

| Abbreviation | Can mean | UTC offset |
|---|---|---|
| CST | Central Standard Time (US) | −6 |
| CST | China Standard Time | +8 |
| CST | Cuba Standard Time | −5 |
| CST | Central Standard Time (Australia) | +9:30 |
| IST | India Standard Time | +5:30 |
| IST | Irish Standard Time | +1 |
| IST | Israel Standard Time | +2 |
| BST | British Summer Time | +1 |
| BST | Bangladesh Standard Time | +6 |

Also: not every zone is on the hour. India is +5:30, Nepal +5:45, Chatham
Islands +12:45, parts of Australia +9:30 / +10:30. Never round a computed time
to the nearest hour — an agent that "cleans up" 14:45 to 15:00 has just created
a 15-minute miss.

---

## Daylight saving: the failure that survives training

DST transitions are not simultaneous worldwide. The US and EU shift three weeks
apart, and the Southern Hemisphere shifts in the opposite direction.

**Worked example — the classic miss.** Owner in Chicago, guest in Berlin,
weekly meeting at 9:00 a.m. Chicago.

| Period | Chicago | Berlin | Berlin local time |
|---|---|---|---|
| Before 9 Mar | CST (UTC−6) | CET (UTC+1) | 16:00 |
| 9 – 29 Mar | CDT (UTC−5) | CET (UTC+1) | **15:00** |
| From 30 Mar | CDT (UTC−5) | CEST (UTC+2) | 16:00 |

The gap window is real, it recurs every year, and an agent working from a
memorised "Berlin is 7 hours ahead" gets it wrong for three weeks. Compute from
the zone database for the actual date, every time.

Related traps:

- **Recurring events** created with a fixed offset drift at every transition.
  Create them with an IANA zone and verify the occurrence on each side of the
  change.
- **"Same time as last time"** — resolve against the stored UTC instant of the
  last meeting, not against the previously stated local hour, if a DST boundary
  has passed since.
- **Guests who travel** between the booking and the meeting. Confirm the zone
  again in the reminder 24 hours out, phrased as a check rather than a question
  ("Still Berlin for Tuesday?").

---

## When you cannot resolve the zone

| Situation | Action |
|---|---|
| New external guest, no zone, no booking link | Block. Send Ask First. Do not create the event. Escalate to the owner after one follow-up with no reply. |
| Known contact with a stored zone, but a suspicious detail (new country, new number) | Proceed with the stored zone, label the assumption in the invite, and add a confirmation line to the 24-hour reminder. |
| Guest gave a zone abbreviation only | Ask once for the city. If they don't reply, use the booking link. Never pick the most likely meaning. |
| Two guests in different zones | State the time in every attendee's zone in the invite body — all of them, not just the owner's. |
| Owner and guest in the same zone | Still apply the two-clock rule. The habit is what prevents the next error. |

**Escalation line to the owner:**
> I don't have [Guest]'s time zone and they haven't confirmed a city. I've held
> the invite rather than guess — can you confirm, or should I send a booking link?

---

## Acceptance tests

An agent has this skill only if it passes all of these.

1. Guest in Berlin, owner in Chicago, meeting proposed for 9:00 a.m. Chicago on
   20 March. Agent states **15:00 Berlin**, not 16:00.
2. Guest writes "CST." Agent asks which city and does not book.
3. Guest in Kathmandu. Agent produces a time ending in **:45**, unrounded.
4. Guest replies "2pm works" with no zone. Agent confirms both clocks before
   sending an invite.
5. Guest's zone is unknown and there is no booking link. Agent creates **no
   event** and escalates.
6. Weekly recurring Chicago→Berlin meeting. Agent verifies the occurrence on
   both sides of 30 March and both land on the intended local hour.
7. Agent reads back a Google Calendar event and the `timeZone` field is
   `America/Chicago`, not `-06:00` and not `Central Standard Time`.
8. Owner and guest both in Toronto. Agent still writes the two-clock line.
9. Booking link used. Agent does not "correct" the slot the guest selected.
10. Guest says "same time as last month," across a DST boundary. Agent converts
    from the stored UTC instant and flags the one-hour change.

---

## Telemetry

Log for every external invite: guest zone, source of the zone (1/2/3), owner
zone, UTC instant, the two rendered local times, and whether the guest's
confirmation was explicit. Review monthly against a single metric — **external
invites later found to be off by any amount**. Target: zero. Current baseline
from last month: 9 of 20.
```

name: guest-timezone-booking
description: Book meetings at the guest's wall-clock time, never the owner's. # Guest-timezone booking

An invite that is one hour off is worse than no invite: the guest shows up, the owner doesn't.
This skill exists so that the *guest's* local time is the source of truth for every external
meeting, regardless of which calendar the owner uses.

## When to use

Use this skill for every event where an attendee is not the owner. That includes meetings that
"look local" — the guest may be travelling, newly relocated, or working from another office.

## Non-negotiable rules

1. **No zone, no booking.** You may not create an external event until you hold an IANA time zone
   identifier for the guest *for the meeting date*. If you cannot establish it, stop and ask.
2. **Never default to the owner's zone.** Not as a fallback, not as a "probably fine", not while
   waiting for a reply. An unresolved zone is a blocked booking.
3. **Never convert from an abbreviation.** `CST`, `IST`, `BST`, `EST`, `PST`, `ET`, `MT` are all
   ambiguous across countries and, for `IST`/`BST`, across hemispheres. Expand to a city or an
   IANA name and read it back to the guest.
4. **Never use the host machine's zone.** Do not read the server's or the agent's local zone and
   assume it is either party's zone. Both parties' zones are explicit inputs.
5. **Store the instant, not the offset.** Persist a UTC instant plus the guest's IANA zone plus
   the guest's original wording. Never persist a fixed offset (`UTC-7`); offsets are not stable
   across DST or across legislative changes.
6. **Every external meeting produces a calendar invite** with the guest as an attendee — or, if
   the calendar cannot invite external attendees, a written confirmation containing both zones.
   A chat message saying "see you Tuesday" is not a booking.
7. **Read back before you confirm.** After writing, fetch the event and re-render it in the
   guest's zone. If it does not match, fix it before the guest is told anything.
8. **A guest's zone is a property of the meeting, not of the contact record.** Contacts move and
   travel. Confirm the zone against the meeting date.

## Procedure

### Step 1 — Establish the guest's zone for the meeting date

Work down this ladder and stop at the first rung that yields a confirmed IANA zone:

1. **Guest record.** An IANA `timezone` field on the contact in the CRM. Treat as a hint only —
   still confirm it in the invite text.
2. **Ask for a city, not a zone.** "Which city will you be in for this meeting?" A city resolves
   to one IANA zone far more reliably than any abbreviation. Ask about the *meeting date*, not
   today, if the meeting is more than a week out or they mention travel.
3. **Guest volunteers an abbreviation.** Do not map it. Reply with the full zone name and a city
   and ask for a yes: "Just to be sure — 3:00 PM India Standard Time (Asia/Kolkata, UTC+5:30)?"
4. **Nothing works.** Do not book. Tell the owner the zone is unresolved and what you asked.

### Step 2 — Convert

Use a maintained IANA time zone database (tzdata released within the last six months). Do not
hardcode offsets or DST rules for any zone. Recent changes that break hardcoded assumptions
include Mexico's 2022 DST abolition, Egypt's 2023 reinstatement, and Iran's 2022 abolition — and
there will be more.

Compute the UTC instant from the guest's local wall time and the guest's zone. Then render that
instant in the owner's zone.

### Step 3 — Validate against DST

Before writing, check the guest's local time against the guest's zone on that date:

- **Gap (time does not exist).** The requested local time is skipped by a spring-forward
  transition. Do not silently shift it. Propose the neighbouring valid times and ask.
- **Overlap (time occurs twice).** The requested local time happens twice at a fall-back
  transition. State both readings with their offsets and ask which one; if the guest is
  unreachable and you must proceed, use the first (pre-transition) occurrence and say so
  explicitly in the invite body.
- **Recurring events.** Store the IANA zone and the local rule ("09:00 America/New_York"), never
  a UTC offset. US and EU DST transitions are two to three weeks apart, so a weekly cross-zone
  meeting shifts by an hour for part of the year. Re-verify each occurrence across a transition.

### Step 4 — Write to the calendar with an explicit zone

The calendar must support, at minimum:

- writing an event with an explicit IANA zone and an unambiguous instant;
- reading the event back;
- rendering any instant in an arbitrary zone.

Adapter rules:

| Calendar | Fields | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| Google Calendar API | `start.dateTime`, `start.timeZone` | `dateTime` as RFC 3339 **with the correct offset**, and `timeZone` as the guest's IANA name. Send both and make them agree. |
| Microsoft Graph / Outlook | `start.dateTime`, `start.timeZone` | `dateTime` is a **naive wall time interpreted in `timeZone`**. There is no offset to catch you out — a wrong `timeZone` silently moves the meeting. If the tenant requires Windows zone names, map IANA→Windows and verify the mapped name: the mapping is many-to-many. `America/New_York`→`Eastern Standard Time` but `America/Indiana/Indianapolis`→`US Eastern Standard Time`; `America/Phoenix`→`US Mountain Standard Time` while `America/Denver`→`Mountain Standard Time`. |
| CalDAV / iCal | `DTSTART`, `VTIMEZONE` | Emit UTC (`…Z`) on the wire where the client permits, and include `VTIMEZONE` if you emit a `TZID`. Guests' clients render UTC in their own zone correctly. |
| Anything else, or unknown | — | Fallback: write the UTC instant, and put both zones in the event title and body. Never let the tool choose the zone. |

### Step 5 — Read back and re-render

Fetch the created event. Render its start in the guest's zone and in the owner's zone. Compare
against what the guest agreed to. Any mismatch — including a one-minute mismatch, which usually
signals a zone coercion — means the event is wrong: fix it before proceeding. Do not confirm to
the guest until the read-back matches.

### Step 6 — Compose the confirmation

Title and body must let the guest verify without converting anything:

```
Subject: <Topic> — <h:mm AM/PM> <Guest Zone Long Name>

When:  <Weekday>, <Month D, YYYY>, <h:mm AM/PM> <Guest Zone Long Name> (<IANA>)
       = <h:mm AM/PM> <Owner Zone Long Name> (<IANA>)
       = <YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ> UTC
Where: <location or dial-in>

The time above is <City> time. If that isn't your local time on <date>,
reply and I'll move it — no need to work it out yourself.
```

Include the UTC line. It costs nothing and it is the one line that survives every client,
every screenshot, and every forwarded email.

### Step 7 — Log the booking

One record per external meeting, appended to the course's booking log:

```json
{
  "event_id": "...",
  "created_at": "2025-01-10T14:02:11Z",
  "guest_name": "...",
  "guest_zone_iana": "America/Denver",
  "guest_zone_source": "asked_city",
  "guest_wording": "10am my time Tuesday",
  "guest_local": "2025-01-14T10:00:00-07:00",
  "owner_zone_iana": "Europe/London",
  "owner_local": "2025-01-14T17:00:00+00:00",
  "utc_instant": "2025-01-14T17:00:00Z",
  "dst_check": "ok",
  "readback_verified": true,
  "calendar": "google|graph|caldav|other"
}
```

`guest_zone_source` and `guest_wording` are the audit trail. When an invite is later disputed,
they answer "what did the guest actually say, and how did we interpret it?"

## Definition of done — a single booking

- [ ] Guest's IANA zone held, for the meeting date, from a named source
- [ ] No abbreviation was converted by assumption
- [ ] DST gap/overlap check run; result recorded
- [ ] Event written with explicit zone and offset that agree
- [ ] Read-back matches the guest's stated local time
- [ ] Invite body shows guest zone, owner zone, and UTC
- [ ] Log record appended

| Zone never captured | Invite in owner's time | Rule 1 (blocked booking) |
| Abbreviation misread | Off by 1–13 hours | Rule 3 |
| API coerced the zone | Off by 1 hour, no error | Step 5 read-back |
| Hardcoded offset | Correct until a DST change | Rule 5, Step 2 |
| DST gap | Meeting at a time that never existed | Step 3 |
| Recurring drift | Correct weekly, off for 2–3 weeks a year | Step 3, recurring rule |
| No invite at all | Guest misses the call | Rule 6 |

## Regression cases

Every agent using this skill must pass all eight before it books a real meeting.

| 1 | Guest in Denver asks for "10am Tuesday 14 Jan 2025"; owner in London | Book 10:00 `America/Denver` = 17:00 `Europe/London`. Both zones in invite. |
| 2 | Guest says "3pm IST" | Do **not** convert. Ask: India (`Asia/Kolkata`), Ireland (`Europe/Dublin`), or Israel (`Asia/Jerusalem`)? |
| 3 | Guest in `America/New_York`, requests 2025-03-09 02:30 | Time does not exist (spring forward). Refuse to book; propose 01:30 or 03:30. |
| 4 | Guest in `America/New_York`, requests 2025-11-02 01:30 | Time occurs twice. Present both offsets (EDT −04:00 / EST −05:00) and ask. |

| 7 | Weekly 09:00 `America/New_York`, owner in `Europe/London`, series spanning late March | Flags that the UTC instant moves for the 2–3 weeks when only one side has transitioned. |
| 8 | Guest says "same time as you", but is in `America/Phoenix` and owner in `America/Denver`, in July | "Same" is not a zone. Confirm the guest's zone; they differ by an hour when Denver is on DST. |

## Acceptance metric

Target: **0 of 20 off, 0 missed calls**, measured from the booking log's
