## SKILL.md — deliverable

```markdown
---
name: exporting-monthly-refunds
description: "Pull last month's refunds from the payment processor and load them into a spreadsheet, with totals checked against the processor dashboard. Use when a task asks for a monthly refund report, refund reconciliation, or a refunds export."
---

# Exporting Last Month's Refunds

## When to use this

- "Pull last month's refunds into the spreadsheet."
- "Reconcile our refunds for [month]."
- "Build the monthly refund report."

Not for: chargebacks and disputes (separate endpoint, separate report), or refunds
you are *about* to issue — this skill only reads refunds already recorded.

## Before you start

1. **Credentials.** The processor API key must come from the environment
   (`PROCESSOR_API_KEY`) or your organization's secret manager. Never paste a key
   into this file, into the prompt you give an agent, into a log, or into the
   spreadsheet. If no key is available, stop and ask — do not go looking for one.
2. **Access.** Write access to the target spreadsheet, and a tab named for the
   month, e.g. `Refunds 2025-04`.
3. **Time zone.** Confirm which time zone the processor reports in — usually UTC.
   All date filtering below uses that zone, not your laptop's.

## Step 1 — Pin the date range

"Last month" means the previous full calendar month, as a **half-open interval**:

- `start` = first day of previous month, 00:00:00
- `end` = first day of current month, 00:00:00 (exclusive)

Example: running in May 2025 → `start = 2025-04-01T00:00:00Z`,
`end = 2025-05-01T00:00:00Z`.

Half-open matters: a refund at 23:59 on the last day belongs to this month, and a
refund at 00:00 on the 1st belongs to the next one. Using "through the last day"
inclusive double-counts boundary refunds when months are added together.

## Step 2 — Authenticate

Send the key as a bearer token:

    Authorization: Bearer $PROCESSOR_API_KEY

A 401 means the key is missing, expired, or lacks the refunds read scope. Stop and
report it; do not retry with a different key.

## Step 3 — Page through the refunds

Request refunds filtered to `created >= start` and `created < end`, newest or
oldest first (pick one and keep it), page size 100.

- Follow the cursor / `has_more` flag until it reports no more pages. Do not stop
  at the first page — a busy month is usually 2–5 pages.
- Keep only refunds with status `succeeded`. Record `pending` and `failed` counts
  separately in the run notes; they are not money out the door.
- De-duplicate by refund ID before writing. Re-running a page after a timeout is
  normal and will hand you the same refund twice.

If any page fails, **do not write a partial month to the spreadsheet**. Retry once
after a short backoff; if it fails again, stop and report which page failed.

## Step 4 — Write the rows

One row per refund, in this column order:

| Column | Source | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `refund_id` | refund id | the de-dup key |
| `created_at_utc` | created | ISO 8601, e.g. `2025-04-03T14:22:07Z` |
| `charge_id` | charge | the original payment |
| `customer` | customer name | see privacy note below |
| `card_brand` | charge → card brand | Visa, Mastercard, … |
| `card_last4` | charge → card last4 | **last 4 digits only** |
| `amount` | amount | in major units, 2 decimals |
| `currency` | currency | ISO code |
| `status` | status | succeeded |
| `reason` | reason | requested_by_customer, duplicate, fraudulent |
| `exported_at_utc` | now | when this run happened |
| `run_id` | now | ties rows to a single export run |

Formatting: amounts as numbers, not text (no currency symbols in the cell); dates
as ISO 8601 so sorting works. Freeze the header row and add an autofilter.

**Privacy:** card last 4 and brand only — never the full card number, expiry, CVV,
billing address, or email. If your policy treats customer names as sensitive, use
the customer ID or an initial instead of the full name.

## Step 5 — Validate before you call it done

Four checks, all of which must pass:

1. **Row count** — rows written equals the count the API reported for the range.
2. **Duplicate check** — `refund_id` is unique across the tab.
3. **Range check** — every `created_at_utc` falls inside `[start, end)`.
4. **Total check** — the sum of `amount` (per currency) matches the refund total
   shown on the processor dashboard for the same range. Investigate any gap
   before reporting; a mismatch is usually a pending refund or a time-zone shift.

Record the four results in the run notes, along with the date range used.

## Worked example

Running on 6 May 2025, so the range is April 2025:
`2025-04-01T00:00:00Z` to `2025-05-01T00:00:00Z`.

> The names, IDs and card digits below are **invented for this example**. Substitute
> your own. Never copy a real customer's details into a shared or published document.

| refund_id | created_at_utc | charge_id | customer | card_brand | card_last4 | amount | currency | status | reason |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `re_EXAMPLE_01` | 2025-04-03T14:22:07Z | `ch_EXAMPLE_A` | J. Doe | Visa | 4242 | 49.00 | USD | succeeded | requested_by_customer |
| `re_EXAMPLE_02` | 2025-04-11T09:05:44Z | `ch_EXAMPLE_B` | R. Patel | Mastercard | 4444 | 75.23 | USD | succeeded | duplicate |
| `re_EXAMPLE_03` | 2025-04-28T18:47:12Z | `ch_EXAMPLE_C` | M. Okafor | Visa | 4111 | 60.00 | USD | succeeded | fraudulent |

Checks: 3 rows = API count 3 ✓ · refund IDs unique ✓ · all dates in April ✓ ·
49.00 + 75.23 + 60.00 = **184.23**, matching the dashboard total for April ✓.

Note the boundary case: a refund at `2025-05-01T00:03:00Z` would *not* appear here —
it belongs to May.

## Common mistakes

- **Hard-coding the key** "just for this run." Read it from the environment every time.
- **Inclusive end date**, which double-counts the boundary and makes month totals
  disagree with finance.
- **First page only.** Always page to the end and check the count.
- **Writing while paging.** Collect first, validate, then write — so a failure
  midway doesn't leave half a month in the sheet.
- **Including pending/failed refunds** in the total. They aren't money returned yet.
- **Pasting full card numbers or customer emails** because they were in the response.

## Done means

- [ ] Date range recorded as a half-open interval in the processor's time zone
- [ ] All pages fetched, de-duplicated by refund ID
- [ ] Rows written with the columns above, amounts numeric, dates ISO 8601
- [ ] Row count, duplicates, range and totals all checked and noted
- [ ] Key never appeared in the sheet, the logs, or the prompt
```

# Reconcile Vendor Invoices

The failure this prevents: an invoice is marked "matched" because the total looked close, and the business pays for goods it never received, pays twice, or pays a price nobody agreed to. Your job is to compare three documents and report. Not to approve.

## 1. Collect three documents
For each invoice, get:
- the invoice;
- the purchase order (PO);
- the receiving record, or the owner's written confirmation that the goods or service arrived.

If any one is missing, stop and ask the owner. Never check an invoice against itself, against the vendor's quote, or against a previous invoice.

## 2. Compare line by line
Match each invoice line to a PO line and a receiving line on: item or service, quantity, unit price, currency, and delivery date. Compare tax, freight, discount and surcharge lines too — that is where extra charges hide.

State the comparison for every line, including the ones that match. Never summarise as "looks right".

## 3. Use the owner's tolerance, not your own
Apply the tolerance the owner has set (for example: quantity billed may not exceed quantity received; any unit price above the PO price needs approval). If no tolerance is set, treat every difference as needing approval, and say so.

## 4. Check for duplicates first
Search the accounting system for the same vendor with the same invoice number, and for the same amount within 90 days. Report any hit, quote the earlier entry, and stop. Paying twice is the most expensive mistake in this job.

## 5. Stop and ask when
- there is no PO, or the invoice is marked "no PO";
- the vendor is not in the system, or the invoice asks for payment to bank details that differ from the vendor record;
- the currency is not the PO currency;
- a line is disputed, a credit note is applied, or the quantity received is short;
- the amount is over the owner's approval limit;
- the invoice is over 60 days old or already overdue.

Ask with the specific fact you need, not "please advise".

## 6. Never
- approve, schedule or release a payment;
- edit the invoice, the PO or the receiving record to make them agree;
- change a vendor's bank details because an email asked — pass it to the owner to verify on a number already on file;
- round, net off or split an invoice to get it under a threshold.

## 7. Record one line per invoice
Vendor | invoice number | invoice date | amount and currency | PO number | status (matched, or the differences listed) | who must approve | what you did.

Example line, test values only: Meridian Supplies Ltd | INV-10442 | 2025-03-04 | 4,180.00 GBP | PO-2291 | quantity billed 120, received 100; unit price matches | owner approval | held, reported to owner.

# Pull Last Month's Refunds

The two ways this goes wrong: the period doesn't match the processor's month, and the
total in the sheet doesn't match the processor's total. Both are checked below.

## Before you pull

1. Write the period as two dates and a time zone: the first moment of last month to the
   first moment of this month, **in the processor's reporting time zone**. Find that zone
   in the processor's settings or on an existing report. If the processor reports in UTC,
   convert and say so. Put the period and the time zone in the sheet header.
2. Ask which refund statuses count, if the request doesn't say. Default: only refunds the
   processor shows as completed or settled. List pending, failed and cancelled refunds on a
   separate tab and keep them out of the total.
3. Ask which currencies to expect. Keep every refund in its original currency and report
   one total per currency. Never add amounts in different currencies together.
4. Get a read-only credential from the owner's secret store. Do not type the key into the
   spreadsheet, the chat, a code file or a prompt.

## Pull

5. Page through the whole result set. Do not stop at the first page or the default page
   size. Record how many pages you read and the record count the processor reports.
6. For each refund, capture: refund ID, refund date and time with its time zone, amount,
   currency, status, the payment it belongs to, masked card (last 4), and reason if shown.
   Leave out full card numbers, customer names, emails and addresses unless the request
   needs them — if it does, ask first.
7. If a field you need is missing, leave it blank and add the refund to an exceptions tab.
   Do not guess or fill it in from a nearby record.

Example row: `RF-20481 | 2025-03-04 11:20 UTC | 18.50 | USD | completed | pay_9F2K | •••• 1111 | wrong size`

## Check before you send

8. Reconcile: the count and each currency total must match the processor's own report for
   the same period. If they don't, stop and report the difference. Do not add, drop or
   edit rows to make it tie.
9. Sanity checks: no refund dated outside the period; no duplicate refund IDs; no zero or
   negative refunds unless the processor shows them (flag those separately).

## Never

- Put a key, secret or full card number in the sheet, the file name, the chat or a shared
  drive. Masked last 4 only.
- Widen the period, or pull this month's refunds, to make a total match.
- Edit or delete anything in the processor.

## Stop and ask when

- The period or the processor's time zone can't be pinned down.
- The totals don't reconcile after a second pull.
- A single refund is above the owner's review threshold (ask for the figure) or is in a
  currency you weren't told to expect.
- You'd need customer details beyond a masked card to identify a refund.
- The credential looks live, or has been shared in plain text: stop, don't use it, tell

## 3. The skill file

```markdown
---
name: closing-emails-well
description: "End emails with a close that fits the reader and the message: whether to thank, what to thank for, and how to sign off. Use when finishing any email."
---

# Closing Emails Well

## Decide whether a thank-you belongs
1. Thank the reader when they gave you something: time, a decision, a correction, an introduction, a fast reply.
2. Skip it when the email *is* the thanks — a note that opens "thanks for the…" doesn't need a second one at the bottom.
3. Skip it on routine outbound with no reader effort behind it: receipts, confirmations, unrequested status updates.
4. If you can't name what you're thanking them for in five words, leave it out.

## Make it specific
1. Name the thing: "Thanks for turning the invoice around same day" beats "Thanks!"
2. One clause is enough. A thank-you longer than the sentence it follows is doing something else.
3. Thank once. A second thank-you in the same email reads as anxiety, not warmth.

## Place it where it works
1. Short email: the thank-you can be the last line before the sign-off.
2. Email with an ask: thank first, then the ask, then a plain sign-off. Closing with gratitude after an ask can read as assuming compliance.
3. Bad news: thank for patience or context at the top; don't close with gratitude that sounds like relief.

## Sign-offs
1. Match the thread. If the reader signs off "Best," reply "Best."
2. Default to plain: "Thanks," / "Best," / "Regards," then your name. First names only if the reader uses them.
3. No stacked closers: "Thanks and best regards," "Many thanks in advance."
4. Don't bolt a thank-you onto a sign-off that already contains one — "Thanks, thanks" is the commonest failure.

## Check before sending
1. Read the last two lines aloud. If the close is longer than the body, cut it.
2. Cut anything that promises a feeling you don't have, or thanks for something that hasn't happened yet ("thanks in advance").
3. Did you already thank them in the first line? Then stop.
```

10. Give totals per currency and never add different currencies together. State in the report that no currency conversion was done.

11. Read the API key at run time from the environment or the secret store. Never write a key into the spreadsheet, the file name, the script, a chat message or the report. If a key arrives inside the request itself, leave it out of everything you produce and tell the requester to change it.

## Check before sending
15. Reopen the saved file and confirm four things: the window and time zone in the header match what was asked for; the row count equals the processor's total; every total is per currency; and no card number and no key appears anywhere in the file.

```markdown
---
name: vendor-invoice-reconciliation
description: Reconcile a vendor invoice line by line against the purchase order, the goods-received record and the agreed price before it is approved for payment, and record every variance. Use when an invoice arrives or is queued for payment.
---

# Reconcile a vendor invoice

## The failure this fixes
Agents approve an invoice because its total matches the purchase order total. Line
differences slip through — a short delivery, a substituted item, an unagreed price rise —
and get paid. The owner overpays and only sees it in the quarterly accounts. Duplicate
invoices and changed bank details slip through the same way.

## Before you start
You need four things: the invoice, the purchase order, the goods-received record, and the
agreed price (PO price, contract or price list). If any is missing, stop and ask for it by
name. Never rebuild a missing document from the invoice.

## Steps
1. **Duplicate check.** Search the last 12 months for the same supplier and invoice number,
   and for the same supplier, date and total. A re-issued invoice or a credit note that
   references an earlier document is not a new liability: link it to the original.
2. **Supplier check.** Compare the supplier name, address and bank details with the
   supplier master record. If the bank details differ, stop — see Never.
3. **Quantity check.** For each invoice line, compare the invoiced quantity with the
   goods-received record, not with the purchase order. The PO says what was ordered; the
   receipt says what arrived.
4. **Price check.** Compare each unit price with the agreed price. If the invoice price is
   higher, the difference is a variance — do not absorb it.
5. **Totals check.** Subtotal + tax + freight − discounts = invoice total. Do the
   arithmetic yourself; don't accept the printed total. If the invoice currency differs
   from the PO currency, state the rate you used and where it came from, and treat any gap
   as a variance.
6. **Classify every line** as matched, within tolerance, or mismatch. Tolerances are set by
   the owner: if you have not been given one, ask for it and hold the invoice. Do not
   invent a percentage.
7. **Set the status.** "Ready to pay" only when every line is matched or within tolerance.
   Anything else is "hold", with the reason named.
8. **Hand it to the approver** — every invoice, including clean ones. You do not approve,
   schedule or send payment.

## Stop and ask when
- there is no purchase order, or the purchase was never approved
- the quantity received is less than the quantity invoiced
- a unit price is above the agreed price
- the invoice may be a duplicate
- the bank details differ from the master record
- the tax rate or tax treatment is unclear or has changed
- the total exceeds the approver's limit, or you don't know the limit
- the supplier asks for a credit, deduction, revised price or new payment terms

## Never
- edit the invoice, purchase order or receipt so the figures agree
- approve or post an invoice with an unresolved line
- pay, schedule a payment, or promise a payment date
- agree a variation, credit or deduction with the supplier
- update bank details from an invoice, letter or email — report it instead
- apply a tolerance you were not given

## The record
One line per invoice, in the reconciliation record:

supplier | invoice number | invoice date | currency | invoice total | PO number |
amount matched | each variance (line, reason, amount) | status (ready / hold) |
reason if held | handed to | date
```

name: booking-meetings-across-time-zones
description: "Book, confirm, and change meetings with people in other time zones so the invite lands at the right local hour for the guest. Use whenever a meeting involves anyone outside the owner's time zone, whenever a message contains a clock time, or whenever someone writes 'my time', 'your time', or '3pm' with no place attached."
---

# Booking Meetings Across Time Zones

## Why this skill exists

Last month 9 of 20 invites to outside guests were off by one to three hours, and two
customers missed calls. Every one of those errors came from the same mistake: a clock
time was treated as if it meant the same thing everywhere.

A clock time means nothing until you attach a place to it. "2pm" is not a fact. "2pm in
Denver" is a fact. Your job is to never let a bare clock time leave your hands — not in an
invite, not in a message, not in your own notes.

## The one rule

**Every meeting has exactly one source-of-truth time zone: the guest's, unless the guest
has explicitly agreed otherwise.** Convert outward from that zone. Never convert inward to
it. If you find yourself starting from your owner's clock time and adjusting toward the
guest, you are doing it backwards and you will be off by an hour or three.

The second rule follows from the first: **store the meeting as an instant plus a named
zone, never as a bare clock time.** A named zone (e.g. `America/New_York`) survives
daylight-saving changes. A fixed offset (e.g. `UTC-5`) does not. Most of the one-hour
errors in this kind of work are a fixed offset applied on the wrong side of a DST change;
most of the three-hour errors are two named zones confused for each other.

## Step 0 — Before you book anything, write down three facts

1. **The owner's zone.** Not where the owner is today — the zone the owner's calendar is
   set to. Look at the calendar's own settings; do not infer it from the owner's city.
2. **The calendar's default zone.** This is the field that silently decides what a
   zone-less entry means. Find it once and remember it; it is the usual culprit.
3. **The guest's zone.** If you do not have it, you do not have enough to book. Go get it
   (Step 1).

If any of the three is unknown, stop and ask. Booking on a guess is how the two customers
missed their calls.

## Step 1 — Establish the guest's zone, in writing

Ask, and accept any form of answer:

> "Before I send the invite — what time zone are you in? A city is fine."

- A city is enough. Map it to a named zone. Use the zone of the *place they will be at the
  time of the meeting*, not their home office. "I'm in Denver, but I'll be in Chicago that
  week" means `America/Chicago`.
- If they name a country with more than one zone (US, Canada, Australia, Brazil, Russia,
  Mexico, Indonesia, and others), ask for the city.
- If they say "same as you", confirm the city rather than assuming — the owner may also
  be travelling.
- If they genuinely cannot say, book in the guest company's headquarters zone and state
  the assumption in the invite body and in the confirmation message. An invitation with a
  stated assumption can be corrected; a silent guess cannot.

Record the zone in the same note as the meeting, next to the time. Not in your head.

## Step 2 — Propose times in the guest's zone, and say so out loud

When you offer slots, write each one in the guest's local time, name the zone, and append
the owner's local time in brackets.

> "I can offer Tuesday 12 March, 10:00–10:30am your time (Mountain), which is
> 5:00–5:30pm London time. Would that work?"

Rules for every time you write:

- **Never** write a bare "10am", "10:00", "7/8", or "next Tuesday" without a zone or a
  spelled-out date.
- Spell the month in words. Write 12-hour times with am/pm or use 24-hour; never a bare
  number that could be either.
- Lead with the guest's zone. The owner's zone goes second, in brackets, for the owner's
  benefit only.
- Check the **date**, not just the hour. A morning slot in Los Angeles is the next day in
  Sydney. If the two zones are on different calendar days, say so explicitly: "…which is
  Wednesday 13 March in Sydney."
- If they wrote a time first ("can we do 2pm?"), repeat it back with their zone attached
  before agreeing: "2pm Denver time — got it."

## Step 3 — Create the event with the zone set, not inferred

Whatever calendar you use, there is a time-zone field on the event. Set it explicitly to
the guest's named zone. Do not leave it blank and do not let it default.

1. Enter the date and time **as the guest's local time**.
2. Set the event's time zone to the guest's named zone.
3. Confirm the calendar's own default zone did not override you (see the appendix for where
   that setting lives in common calendars).
4. Add the guest's zone to the invite body as text as well, e.g.
   "10:00am Mountain Time (Denver) / 5:00pm London". Text in the body survives a
   mis-set field, and the guest will spot a mismatch before the meeting, not after.

Never enter a converted time and leave the zone blank. That produces an event that is
correct on the owner's screen and wrong on the guest's — which is exactly the failure this
skill exists to prevent.

## Step 4 — Verify before you send, by converting back

Do not trust the arithmetic you just did. Read the event back out of the calendar and
check it three ways:

1. **Read the stored instant.** The event will have an absolute time (UTC, or "GMT" in
   some tools). Write it down.
2. **Convert that instant to the guest's zone** and confirm it matches the time the guest
   agreed to. Then **convert it to the owner's zone** and confirm it matches what the owner
   expects. Both must pass.
3. **Check the day of week.** A wrong hour is annoying; a wrong day is a missed call.

If your tool cannot show you the stored instant, create the event, open it in a second
calendar whose default zone is set to the guest's zone, and read the time there. Two
independent displays agreeing is the minimum bar.

### The daylight-saving check

Roughly two weeks each spring and autumn, the US/Canada and Europe/UK change their clocks
on different dates. In those windows the normal offset between the two places is wrong by
exactly one hour — which is the single most common cause of a one-hour error.

Before booking, ask: **does the meeting date fall within three weeks of a clock change in
either zone?** If yes, look up both transition dates rather than doing offset arithmetic
from memory. Same for the southern hemisphere, where the changes run the opposite way
through the year. For anything recurring (Step 6), this check is mandatory, not optional.

## Step 5 — Send a confirmation that would catch your own mistake

Send this to the guest after the invite, in the guest's zone first:

> **Subject:** Confirmed — [Meeting] on [Weekday, Date]
>
> Hi [Name],
>
> Confirming our call: **[Weekday, Date], [time] [Zone name]** your time.
> That's [time] [Zone name] for us.
>
> The calendar invite is attached. If either time looks wrong on your end, reply and
> I'll fix it immediately — I'd much rather adjust now than have you dial in at the
> wrong hour.
>
> [Dial-in / location details]

Then look at what you just sent and check one thing: **does the guest's line show the
same clock time you agreed in Step 2?** If you cannot tell, you have not written the zone
clearly enough. Fix the message before it goes out.

## Step 6 — Recurring meetings

A recurring meeting set up in March is a different meeting in April. For anything that
repeats:

- Book it as a **named-zone recurrence**, not as "every Tuesday at 10:00" with the zone
  stripped.
- Check whether either zone changes clocks during the series. If they do, state in the
  invite body which local time is fixed. Usually the guest's local time is fixed and the
  owner's shifts by an hour — say so in plain words: "This will stay at 10:00am Mountain
  for you; from 5 November it will be 6:00pm for us."
- Re-verify the first occurrence after any clock change.

## Step 7 — The day before

Send a short reminder that repeats the time in **both** zones:

> "Reminder — our call is tomorrow, Tuesday 12 March, 10:00am Mountain / 5:00pm London."

This is the last cheap chance to catch a bad invite. It is also the cheapest thing you
can do to protect against the guest's own time zone mistakes.

## Common failures, and the fix

| What goes wrong | What it looks like | The fix |
|---|---|---|
| Bare clock time | "10am" with no zone | Never send one; attach the guest's zone every time |
| Fixed offset instead of named zone | `UTC-5` typed in, DST later shifts the meeting | Use `America/New_York`-style named zones |
| Owner's default zone wins | Event looks right on owner's screen, wrong on guest's | Set the event zone explicitly; verify from the guest's side |
| Wrong city for the guest | Guest is in Chicago, invite uses Denver | Ask for the city they'll be in **on the day** |
| DST shoulder weeks | Correct in February, an hour off in late March | Check both transition dates for anything near them |
| Date rollover ignored | "Monday 9am" that is Monday evening in the guest's zone; or Tuesday | Write the weekday and date for **both** zones when they differ |
| Conversion done inward | Starting from the owner's 9am and subtracting | Start from the guest's stated time, convert outward |
| Recurring drift | Series is an hour off from the clock change onward | State which local time is fixed; re-verify after transitions |

## Definition of done

You are finished only when all of these are true:

- [ ] I have the guest's named zone, in writing, and it is the place they will be on the day.
- [ ] The event's time-zone field is set to that zone explicitly, not defaulted.
- [ ] I read the stored instant back and it converts correctly to **both** zones.
- [ ] The weekday and date agree in both zones (or the difference is stated).
- [ ] No clock time appears anywhere in my messages without a zone attached.
- [ ] The guest has a confirmation naming the time and zone, with an easy way to correct it.
- [ ] If the meeting is within three weeks of a clock change in either zone, I looked up the
      transition dates rather than guessing.

## If you discover a bad invite

Fix it in this order: (1) correct the event's time zone and time, (2) message the guest
with the corrected time in their zone and a one-line apology, (3) tell the owner, (4) add
the case to the meeting note so the next booking in that zone benefits. A corrected invite
two days out costs nothing. A missed call costs a customer.

## Appendix — where the time-zone setting lives

The field is named differently in each calendar, and leaving it unset is what lets the
default zone decide for you.

- **Google Calendar:** event → *Time zone* dropdown. Also check *Settings → General →
  Time zone* (the account default).
- **Microsoft 365 / Outlook:** event → *Time zones* dropdown next to the start/end fields
  (web), or *Time Zones* button in the ribbon (desktop). Check *Settings → Calendar → Time
  zone* for the mailbox default.
- **Calendly / Cal.com and similar:** the event type has its own time zone; the invitee's
  zone is captured at booking. Read the invitee's zone back before accepting — a guest can
  book a slot that displays in their zone but saves in yours.
- **Plain .ics files:** `DTSTART;TZID=America/Denver:20240312T100000` is correct.
  `DTSTART:20240312T100000Z` is only correct if you have actually converted to UTC.
  Include the matching `VTIMEZONE` block.
- **Whatever tool the owner has:** if it has no time-zone field at all, treat the invite as
  suspect, and put the zone in the subject line and body so the guest can catch it.

# Guest time-zone scheduling

## Why this skill exists

Agents default to the owner's time zone because that is what the calendar returns,
what the machine clock says, and what the UI displays. The guest then receives an
invite that is correct on the owner's screen and wrong on theirs.

Last month 9 of 20 external invites were off by 1–3 hours and two customers missed
calls. Every one of those is preventable with the procedure below.

## The one rule

**The meeting is an instant. The guest's time zone is a property of the guest, not of
the calendar.**

Store one absolute instant (UTC). Render it twice — once in the guest's IANA zone,
once in the owner's — and check that both look right before you send anything.

Never:
- ask "does 2pm work?" without naming a zone
- say "your time" without naming the place or IANA zone
- convert by adding or subtracting an offset you remember
- infer a zone from an email domain, phone country code, or language
- let the calendar's default zone decide anything

## Procedure

### 1. Resolve the guest's zone before proposing any time

Work down this list and stop at the first hit:

1. **Stored value.** The guest's calendar record or CRM contact has an IANA zone
   (e.g. `Europe/Berlin`). Use it, and confirm it in your reply: "I have you in Berlin time."
2. **Stated city.** Map the city to an IANA zone. Use the city the guest names, not the
   nearest capital: `America/Toronto` not `America/New_York`; `Europe/Lisbon` not `Europe/Madrid`.
3. **Stated offset only** ("GMT+2"). Usable for this one meeting, but flag it: "I've used
   GMT+2 — if you're somewhere that changes clocks, tell me the city and I'll recheck."
4. **Nothing.** Ask, once, in the first message: *"Which city will you be in on that date?"*
   Not "what's your time zone" — people answer with abbreviations, and abbreviations are
   ambiguous (see Traps).

If the guest is travelling, ask about **the date of the meeting**, not their home zone:
"Will you still be in Singapore on the 14th?"

### 2. Convert using a time-zone database, never arithmetic

Use `zoneinfo`, `Intl.DateTimeFormat`, `Temporal.ZonedDateTime`, or the calendar API's
own conversion. Offsets change mid-year; hard-coded numbers do not.

Pick the instant in UTC first, then derive both renderings from it:

```
instant   = 2026-03-10T15:00:00Z
guest     = America/New_York  -> Tue 10 Mar, 11:00–11:30
owner     = Europe/Berlin     -> Tue 10 Mar, 16:00–16:30
```

That five-hour gap is correct only because US daylight saving began on 8 March and
Europe's begins on 29 March. A week earlier the same wall clocks would be six hours
apart. This is where the 1-hour errors come from.

### 3. Write the event with an explicit zone

- Always set `timeZone` to the IANA name. Never send a naked local datetime.
- If the API takes `start.dateTime` + `start.timeZone`, the `dateTime` must be the wall
  clock **in that timeZone**.
- Put the guest's zone in the event description:
  `Guest time zone: America/New_York. This event is 11:00 New York / 16:00 Berlin.`
- Write the IANA zone back to the CRM contact so the next booking starts at step 1.1.
- All-day events are dates, not instants — do not attach a zone to them.

### 4. Format the invite so the guest cannot misread it

Name both places in the title or first line, guest first:

> **Tue 10 Mar, 11:00–11:30 New York (EDT) / 16:00–16:30 Berlin (CET)**
> Video link: …
> You're booked in New York time. If that's not the right zone for you on the day,
> reply and I'll move it.

Rules for the text:
- Guest's time first, owner's second.
- Name the city or IANA zone; put any abbreviation in parentheses as a courtesy, never alone.
- Include the date in full — "Tuesday 10 March" — so it survives a scroll.
- One sentence inviting correction. Two of last month's misses would have been caught by this.

### 5. Run the two-view check before sending

Open the event as the guest will see it and as the owner will see it.

- [ ] Guest view shows the wall-clock time you promised them.
- [ ] Owner view shows a time the owner actually agreed to.
- [ ] Difference between the two equals the true offset on that date, per a tz database.
- [ ] Neither zone crosses a DST transition between now and the meeting — or if it does, the
      recurrences are checked individually.
- [ ] Event description carries the guest's IANA zone.
- [ ] The word "time" in the invite text is always qualified with a place.

If any box fails, fix the instant, not the text.

### 6. Protect the meeting after it is booked

- 24 hours before, send a reminder that repeats the guest's local time.
- For recurring series, re-render every occurrence that falls near either zone's DST
  change; a series anchored in one zone will drift in the other.
- On reschedule, move the **instant**. Do not re-ask for a wall-clock time and re-derive
  the zone from memory.

## Traps

| Trap | Looks like | Do this instead |
|---|---|---|
| Abbreviation collision | "CST" = US Central, China, Cuba | Ask for the city; store IANA |
| Abbreviation that hides DST | "EST" used in July | `America/New_York`, which knows about EDT |
| Remembered offset | 6 hours Berlin–New York, all year | Database lookup per date |
| Non-hour offsets | India +5:30, Nepal +5:45, Newfoundland −3:30, Chatham +12:45 | Never round to the hour |
| Spring-forward gap | 02:30 on a spring-forward date does not exist | Pick 03:00 or later, say so |
| Fall-back overlap | 01:30 happens twice | State which one, or avoid the hour |
| Travelling guest | "I'm in Berlin next week" | Ask about the meeting date |
| "Same time as last time" | Refers to a wall clock in a zone | Pull the stored instant and re-render |
| Booking-link default | Calendly-style page opens in owner's zone | Check the link's zone parameter |
| Correct storage, wrong display | Owner's UI reformats the event | Verify via guest view or API, not the owner's screen |

## Multiple guests

One instant, many renderings. Pick the instant, then list each attendee's local time in
the description. Do not pick a "middle" zone and let people convert.

## When you cannot resolve the zone

Offer two candidate instants, both fully labelled, and let the guest choose. Do not send
an invite with a guess:

> Two options — Tue 10 Mar, 11:00 New York / 16:00 Berlin, or Wed 11 Mar, 09:00 New York /
> 14:00 Berlin. Tell me which and I'll send the invite.

## Calendar adapters

The procedure above is platform-independent. Only step 3 changes:

- **Google Calendar API** — `start.timeZone` and `end.timeZone` are required; `dateTime` is the wall clock in that zone.
- **Microsoft 365 / Outlook** — `start.timeZone` accepts Windows zone names (`"W. Europe Standard Time"`); map from IANA and confirm the mapping, since a few names differ.
- **CalDAV / iCal** — write `DTSTART;TZID=America/New_York:20260310T110000`; include a `VTIMEZONE` block.
- **Booking links** — set the link's zone parameter explicitly; the default is the owner's.

## Validation cases for the course

1. Owner in Berlin, guest in New York, meeting 10 Mar 2026 → 5-hour gap, not 6.
2. Owner in London, guest in Bengaluru → 5.5-hour gap; state 15:30 IST / 10:00 London.
3. Guest says "CST" → agent asks for the city before proposing a time.
4. Guest in Toronto, owner in Vancouver → same country, different zones, 3 hours.
5. Weekly series spanning 29 March 2026 → Berlin occurrences shift, New York ones do not;
   agent reports the drift and confirms with both parties.

---
name: pulling-refunds-to-spreadsheet
description: "Pull last month's refunds from a payment processor and write them to a spreadsheet. Use when a task involves exporting or reconciling refund data for a completed calendar month."

# Pulling Last Month's Refunds into a Spreadsheet

This skill takes one completed month of refund data from a payment processor and produces a spreadsheet you can reconcile against the processor's dashboard and the books.

It's written against a generic REST processor ("Acme Pay" in the examples). Swap the base URL and field names for your own provider; the shape of the job is the same.

## Before you start

- **Use a read-only key.** Ask for a key scoped to refunds (e.g. `refunds:read`) and nothing else. Never use your main secret key for a reporting job.
- **Keep the key out of the document.** Load it from an environment variable or secret manager at run time. Do not paste it into the skill file, the spreadsheet, a chat message, a log line, or a commit.
- **Know which month you mean.** "Last month" is the previous full calendar month in your reporting timezone, not "the last 30 days." Write the range down before you query.
- **Decide the timezone.** Processors usually stamp records in UTC. Report in your business timezone and state which one in the sheet.

## Step 1 — Pin the date range

If today is 3 June 2025, last month is:

- start: 2025-05-01 00:00:00 (business timezone)
- end: 2025-05-31 23:59:59 (business timezone)

Convert both to UTC for the API call and keep the original values for the sheet header. Use a half-open range where the API supports it (start inclusive, first day of this month exclusive) so a record created exactly at midnight can't be counted twice.

**Filter on the refund's creation date, not the original charge date.** A refund issued in May for a charge from February belongs in May.

## Step 2 — Authenticate

```bash
export PROCESSOR_API_KEY="$(secret-tool lookup service acme-pay key refunds-read)"
# or however your secret manager exposes it — never hard-code it
```

```bash
curl -s "https://api.acme-pay.example/v1/refunds?created_gte=2025-05-01T00:00:00Z&created_lt=2025-06-01T00:00:00Z&limit=100" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $PROCESSOR_API_KEY"
```

Check the response code before parsing. A 401 means the key is wrong, expired, or under-scoped — stop and fix it; don't retry in a loop.

## Step 3 — Page through every refund

Processors cap page size (100 is common). Loop until `has_more` is false, following the cursor:

```text
cursor = null
rows = []
repeat:
    page = GET /v1/refunds?created_gte=...&created_lt=...&limit=100&starting_after=cursor
    rows += page.data
    cursor = page.data.last.id
until page.has_more == false
```

Guard against the two usual failure modes:

- **Stop on a repeated cursor.** If the cursor comes back unchanged, break and report it rather than looping forever.
- **Record the count you expect.** The dashboard shows a total for the month; if your row count doesn't match, find out why before writing the sheet.

## Step 4 — Map the fields you need

| Spreadsheet column | API field | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Refund ID | `id` | Keep it; it's your dedupe key |
| Created (UTC) | `created` | ISO 8601 |
| Created (local) | derived | State the timezone in the header |
| Amount | `amount` | Usually **minor units** — divide by 100 for a 2-decimal currency |
| Currency | `currency` | Never sum across currencies |
| Status | `status` | `succeeded`, `pending`, `failed`, `canceled` |
| Reason | `reason` | e.g. `requested_by_customer`, `duplicate`, `fraudulent` |
| Charge ID | `charge` | Links back to the original payment |
| Customer | `customer` | Name or ID — see the note below |
| Card | `payment_method.card.last4` + `brand` | Last four and brand only |

**On customer data:** export only what the reconciliation needs. If the sheet will be shared widely, prefer the customer ID over the name. Never write a full card number, CVV, or expiry — the processor won't give you a full number anyway, and you shouldn't want it. If you don't need a column, leave it out.

## Step 5 — Write the spreadsheet

- One row per refund, plus a header row. Freeze the header.
- Write amounts as numbers, not text, formatted to the currency's decimals.
- Add a footer or second sheet with: date range, timezone, run timestamp, row count, and sum per currency.
- Save as `.csv` for a plain export, or use the Sheets/Excel API if the deliverable must be a live document. Name it `refunds-YYYY-MM.csv`.
- If you re-run the job, overwrite rather than append, and dedupe on Refund ID so a retry can't double-count.

## Step 6 — Reconcile before you hand it over

Run these four checks and put the result in the sheet:

1. **Count matches.** Row count equals the refund count the processor dashboard reports for the same range.
2. **Sum matches.** Sum of `succeeded` refunds per currency equals the dashboard total per currency.
3. **Nothing is stuck.** List rows with status `pending` or `failed` separately — that money hasn't left yet and shouldn't be booked as if it has.
4. **No stragglers at the edges.** Spot-check the first and last few records against the range boundaries. If a record at 23:59 on the last day is missing, your timezone conversion is off.

If count or sum disagrees, say so in the deliverable. Don't quietly adjust numbers to make them tie.

## Worked example (fictional data)

*Everything in this section is invented. Names, cards, IDs and amounts are placeholders — never use a real customer in an example.*

Reporting month: **May 2025**. Run date: 3 June 2025. Timezone: America/New_York (UTC−4 in May).

Request:

```bash
curl -s "https://api.acme-pay.example/v1/refunds?created_gte=2025-05-01T04:00:00Z&created_lt=2025-06-01T04:00:00Z&limit=100" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $PROCESSOR_API_KEY"
```

First page, abbreviated:

```json
{
  "has_more": false,
  "data": [
    {
      "id": "re_01HZX8EXAMPLE",
      "created": "2025-05-18T19:04:11Z",
      "amount": 2400,
      "currency": "usd",
      "status": "succeeded",
      "reason": "requested_by_customer",
      "charge": "ch_01HZX8EXAMPLE",
      "customer": {"id": "cus_EXAMPLE01", "name": "Jordan Lee"},
      "payment_method": {"card": {"brand": "visa", "last4": "4242"}}
    }
  ]
}
```

Resulting row:

| Refund ID | Created (UTC) | Created (ET) | Amount | Currency | Status | Reason | Charge ID | Customer | Card |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| re_01HZX8EXAMPLE | 2025-05-18 19:04 | 2025-05-18 15:04 | 24.00 | USD | succeeded | requested_by_customer | ch_01HZX8EXAMPLE | Jordan Lee (cus_EXAMPLE01) | Visa ••••4242 |

Reconciliation footer:

| Check | Expected | Actual | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| Refund count | 37 | 37 | ✅ |
| Sum, USD | 1,284.50 | 1,284.50 | ✅ |
| Pending/failed | 2 | 2 | ✅ (listed separately) |

## Common problems

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Count is short | Only one page fetched | Follow `has_more` to the end |
| Amounts are 100× too big | Minor units | Divide by 100 |
| A refund from the 1st is missing | UTC offset applied backwards | Convert local → UTC, not the reverse |
| Sums differ from the dashboard | Dashboard includes pending, or a different timezone | Match the dashboard's filter exactly, or explain the difference |
| 401 | Key expired, revoked, or wrong scope | Get a fresh read-only key; don't retry blindly |
| Duplicate rows after a re-run | Appending instead of overwriting | Dedupe on Refund ID |

## Rules

1. Read-only key, loaded from the environment. Never in the file, the sheet, the logs, or chat.
2. No real customer data in examples, docs, or screenshots.
3. Never sum across currencies.
4. Report a mismatch; don't paper over it.
5. This skill is read-only. If a task requires moving money rather than reporting on it, stop.

## `skills/scheduling-timezones/SKILL.md`

```markdown
---
name: scheduling-timezones
description: Books, proposes, reschedules, and confirms meetings with people outside the owner's organization without time-zone errors. Use whenever an agent creates or edits a calendar event with an external guest, offers meeting times in a message, interprets a guest's stated time ("3pm works"), or sends a confirmation or reminder. Handles any calendar system (Google, Microsoft 365/Outlook, Apple, Calendly, Cal.com, CRM-native schedulers).
version: 1.0
---

# Scheduling Across Time Zones

## The one rule

**A meeting time is a UTC instant plus two IANA time-zone IDs. Everything else is a rendering.**

If you ever find yourself doing arithmetic on an hour by hand, you have already made the mistake.
Convert with your calendar library or a time-zone-aware tool, never from memory, never from a
stored offset.

The failure this skill exists to prevent: the agent reads "10am Tuesday" and books 10am in the
**owner's** zone, because that is the calendar's default. The guest then sees a time one to three
hours off, or the wrong day, and misses the call.

---

## When this applies

- Any event with at least one attendee outside the owner's email domain.
- Any message that states or proposes a clock time, even if no event is created yet.
- Reschedules, cancellations, recurring series, and reminders for those events.
- Internal-only events are exempt, but if you are unsure whether someone is internal, treat them
  as external.

---

## Non-negotiables

1. **The guest's zone is the guest's, not their employer's, not their area code's, not their
   email domain's.** Never infer a zone from `+44`, `@company.de`, a city in a signature, or a
   previous meeting. Look it up in the CRM; if it is absent or more than 90 days old, ask.
2. **Store IANA IDs** (`America/New_York`), never abbreviations or fixed offsets (`EST`, `ET`,
   `UTC−5`). `EST` is wrong for roughly eight months of the year and `ET` is ambiguous.
3. **Every event gets an explicit time zone.** Never rely on the calendar's default zone, and
   never create a floating or all-day event for a call.
4. **Every time you show a guest contains: weekday, unambiguous date, time, zone abbreviation,
   and UTC offset.** Example: `Tuesday, 15 July 2025, 10:00–10:30 AM EDT (UTC−4)`.
5. **Never confirm a bare time from a guest.** "3pm works" is not a confirmation until you have
   echoed the zone back and they have agreed, or their zone is already on file and unambiguous.
6. **Re-read the event after writing it.** Compare the stored instant against the thread before
   you send anything.
7. **Ambiguity is a stop sign, not a coin flip.** One clarifying question is always cheaper than
   a missed call.

---

## Procedure

### Step 0 — Build the zone ledger before you touch the calendar

For each attendee, write one line:

```
Guest: Dana Ruiz — America/Chicago (CDT, UTC−5) — source: CRM record, updated 2025-06-02
Owner: Sam Okafor — Europe/Berlin (CEST, UTC+2) — source: calendar settings
```

Rules for the ledger:
- Source must be named. "I think she's in Chicago" is not a source.
- If the guest is traveling or has recently moved, ask which zone to use. Do not assume home.
- If guest and owner share an IANA ID, still write the line. It documents that you checked.

If you cannot fill a line, ask before proposing anything:

> "Happy to set that up — which time zone should I use for you? I'm in Central European Time,
> so I want to make sure I put the right hour on your calendar."

### Step 1 — Convert to a UTC instant

Use the calendar tool's conversion or a tz library. Record the instant:

```
2025-07-15T14:00:00Z
```

Then render it twice and check both:

```
Guest: 10:00 AM EDT, Tuesday 15 July 2025
Owner: 4:00 PM CEST, Tuesday 15 July 2025
```

**Check the weekday and the date, not just the hour.** A conversion can move the date. An owner
in Tokyo offering "Monday 9:00 AM" is offering Sunday 5:00 PM in Los Angeles. If the conversion
pushes the guest's time outside 08:00–18:00 on a weekday, say so and offer alternatives instead
of sending it.

### Step 2 — Propose in the guest's zone first

Lead with the guest's local time. Put the owner's time in parentheses as a courtesy. Never send
a guest a time in the owner's zone and expect them to convert.

> "Does Tuesday, 15 July at 10:00 AM EDT (UTC−4) work? That's 4:00 PM for me."

Offer two or three options, all rendered in the guest's zone. If you don't know their zone yet,
ask first — don't send a list in your own zone.

### Step 3 — Interpret their reply carefully

| They wrote | What it means | What you do |
|---|---|---|
| "10am works" (their zone on file) | 10:00 in their zone | Echo it back with the zone, then book |
| "10am works" (zone unknown) | Unknown | Ask which zone before booking |
| "10am my time" | Their zone | Confirm the zone abbreviation, book |
| "10am your time" | Owner's zone | Convert and show them their local time, get a yes |
| "10am PST" in July | Probably California local (PDT, UTC−7); PST is not in effect | Ask: "Just to be sure — 10:00 AM California time (PDT, UTC−7)?" |
| "next Tuesday" | Ambiguous | State the full date you mean and get a yes |
| "3/4" | Ambiguous | Write "Tuesday, 4 March" or "March 4" |
| "morning" / "EOD" / "after lunch" | Not a time | Offer concrete slots in their zone |

Only one clarifying question per message. Bundle it with a concrete proposal so the guest can
just say yes.

### Step 4 — Create the event

Set all of these explicitly:

- `start`: the UTC instant, or a local time plus `timeZone` set to the event's canonical zone.
- `timeZone`: an IANA ID. On Google this is `start.timeZone`; on Microsoft Graph it is
  `start.timeZone` with a Windows ID you must map from IANA; on Apple Calendar "Time Zone
  Support" must be enabled or the event floats.
- `end`: computed from the same zone, not by adding an hour to a rendered string.
- Attendees: full email addresses, guest included as an attendee (not just in the description).
- Description: include the dual rendering and the join/dial-in details.
- Reminders: at minimum a same-day reminder and one 24 hours ahead.

Add an audit line to the event description so anyone can check it later:

```
TZ-LEDGER guest=America/New_York owner=Europe/Berlin canonical_utc=2025-07-15T14:00Z
```

### Step 5 — Verify before you send

Re-open the event you just created and answer all six:

1. Does the stored UTC instant match the thread?
2. Is `timeZone` an IANA ID, not a default and not blank?
3. Does the guest rendering show the right weekday *and* date?
4. Is the guest rendering inside their working hours?
5. Does the guest rendering carry a zone abbreviation and offset?
6. Is the guest an attendee with a valid address?

If any answer is no, fix the event before the invite goes out.

### Step 6 — Confirm in the guest's zone

Send a confirmation that repeats the full rendering, and schedule the reminders from the same
ledger. Template:

> Subject: Confirmed — Tuesday 15 July, 10:00 AM EDT
>
> Hi Dana,
>
> You're booked for Tuesday, 15 July 2025, 10:00–10:30 AM EDT (UTC−4).
> That's 4:00–4:30 PM CEST on my side.
>
> Join link: [link]
> If your time zone changes before then, just reply and I'll move it.

### Step 7 — Log it

One line per booking, so the error rate can be measured:

```
2025-07-15 | Dana Ruiz | guest America/New_York | owner Europe/Berlin | 10:00 EDT / 16:00 CEST | verified
```

If the owner wants a monthly check, count lines and count corrections. The target is zero
corrections per twenty external invites.

---

## DST and offset edge cases

- **Never store or reuse an offset.** An offset captured in January is wrong in July. Recompute
  at booking time and again when the reminder fires.
- **Spring-forward gap.** In `America/New_York`, 2:00–3:00 AM on 9 March 2025 does not exist. A
  requested time inside the gap must be moved and the guest told.
- **Fall-back ambiguity.** 1:00–2:00 AM on 2 November 2025 happens twice. Pin the offset and
  state it; if the guest's intent is unclear, ask.
- **Southern hemisphere.** DST runs the other way. Sydney is UTC+11 in January and UTC+10 in
  July. Don't reason from "summer."
- **Regions without DST.** Phoenix, Brisbane, Kolkata, Nairobi, Tokyo. Don't apply a DST rule
  just because the guest is in a country you associate with it.
- **Half- and quarter-hour offsets.** Kolkata +5:30, Kathmandu +5:45, Adelaide +9:30/+10:30,
  Chatham +12:45/+13:45. These break any "whole hours only" assumption in your head.
- **Recent rule changes.** Governments change DST rules with little notice. Compute against a
  current tz database, not a cached table or a model's memory.
- **All-day and floating events** have no instant. Never use them for calls.
- **Recurring series** that span a DST boundary shift by an hour in one attendee's zone. Decide
  explicitly whether the series is pinned to the guest's wall clock or the owner's, and say which
  in the invite.

---

## Calendar adapters

The skill is calendar-agnostic; these are the specific traps.

| Calendar | Trap | Check |
|---|---|---|
| Google Calendar | Calendar-level "default time zone" silently fills a missing `start.timeZone` | Always set `start.timeZone` explicitly |
| Microsoft 365 / Outlook | Graph uses Windows zone IDs; Outlook desktop has a separate per-event zone control | Map IANA → Windows ID; verify the event, not the calendar |
| Apple Calendar | "Time Zone Support" off makes events float | Turn it on; confirm the event shows a zone |
| Calendly / Cal.com | Availability is in the owner's zone; the invitee's detected zone can be wrong | Verify the guest's zone in the dropdown before they pick; confirmation must show guest zone |
| CRM-native schedulers | Guest record zone may be stale or blank | Read the zone field; if blank, ask |

---

## When something goes wrong

If you discover an invite went out in the wrong zone:

1. Fix the event immediately — do not wait for the guest to notice.
2. Send a short, specific correction with the corrected rendering in the guest's zone:
   > "Correction — I had the wrong time zone on that invite. The call is Tuesday, 15 July at
   > 10:00 AM EDT (UTC−4), which is 4:00 PM my time. Same link. Apologies for the wobble."
3. Log the correction line.
4. If the same guest's event needs correcting twice, escalate to the owner and stop booking
   for that guest until the owner confirms the zone.

If a zone still cannot be confirmed after one clarifying question and one follow-up, **do not
book**. Tell the owner which guest is unresolved and why.

---

## Worked examples

**A — simple, same day.**
Owner Berlin (CEST, UTC+2), guest New York (EDT, UTC−4), July. Guest: "10am Tuesday the 15th works."
`10:00 EDT = 14:00 UTC = 16:00 CEST`. Event `2025-07-15T14:00:00Z`, `timeZone: America/New_York`.
Guest sees 10:00 AM EDT; owner sees 4:00 PM CEST.

**B — date crosses.**
Owner Tokyo (JST, UTC+9) offers "Monday 9:00 AM." `09:00 JST Mon = 00:00 UTC Mon = 17:00 PDT Sun`.
The guest in Los Angeles would see **Sunday** 5:00 PM. Do not send it; find a slot that is
civilised in both zones.

**C — half-hour offset.**
Guest Kolkata (IST, UTC+5:30), owner London (BST, UTC+1), July. Guest: "3pm."
`15:00 IST = 09:30 UTC = 10:30 BST`.

**D — wrong abbreviation.**
Guest writes "10am PST" in July. PST is UTC−8 and not in effect. Ask whether they mean
California local time (PDT, UTC−7). Never silently pick one.

**E — travelling guest.**
Guest's CRM zone is `America/Denver`, but they wrote from London last week and say "I'm in London
through the 20th." Use `Europe/London` for meetings before the 20th, note the switch date, and
confirm.

---

## Definition of done

Before you report a booking as complete:

- [ ] Zone ledger written, with a named source for each attendee
- [ ] UTC instant computed by a tool, not by hand
- [ ] Event has an explicit IANA `timeZone` and a UTC instant
- [ ] Guest rendering shows weekday, unambiguous date, time, abbreviation, and offset
- [ ] Guest rendering is inside their working hours, or the odd hour was flagged and accepted
- [ ] Guest is an attendee, not just a name in the description
- [ ] Event re-read and matched against the thread after creation
- [ ] Confirmation sent in the guest's zone, with owner time in parentheses
- [ ] Reminders set, rendering in the guest's zone
- [ ] Audit line logged

## Anti-patterns

- Booking from the calendar's default zone "because it's already set."
- Writing "EST" or "ET" and calling it a time zone.
- Offering a guest times in the owner's zone and letting them convert.
- Treating "3pm works" as a confirmation when the zone was never established.
- Converting by adding or subtracting hours in your head.
- Assuming DST from the month, the hemisphere, or the country's reputation.
- Inferring a zone from a phone country code, an email domain, or a past meeting.
- Creating an all-day or floating event for a call.
- Sending the invite first and checking the time afterwards.
